items.title: How ECI's dubious software branded 3.66 crore voters in West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh as suspects
items.shows: From the Commission's own suspect-list summaries, it shows software flagged about 1.31 crore West Bengal and 2.35 crore Madhya Pradesh electors for 'logical discrepancies' with no written protocol for resolving them.

items.title: ECI misled the Supreme Court on SIR in West Bengal
items.shows: It uses official records and interviews with election officials to argue that the West Bengal notices were produced in bulk by central software, and that registration officers did not review them one by one as the Commission told the Court.

items.title: How EC Has Quietly Changed Form 6 During SIR, Evading Parliament
items.shows: It traces how the Commission changed Form 6 in each round of the SIR, first adding a declaration in Bihar and later altering the online form itself, with no amendment to the rules. Former Commission officials it quotes say only the government can change the form, under the oversight of Parliament.

items.title: Delhi SIR: With More Than Half the Voters in India's Capital Either Purged or on ECI's Doubtful List, VIPs Get a Pass and the Poorest Pay
items.authors: Shubhangi Derhgawen, Dikshya Koirala, Sumedha Mittal
items.shows: From booth-wise lists of names left off and ground reporting, it finds 79.2 lakh of Delhi's 1.45 crore electors were left off the draft or sent a notice, with the heaviest losses among the poorest, including residents of demolished settlements.

items.title: 14 times in 10 months, two Election Commissioners objected on record to poll panel steps
items.shows: From internal notes and letters of November 2025 to August 2026, it shows that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi objected on record at least 14 times to SIR decisions, including the Form 6 change, centralised control of the roll software and the West Bengal appeals.

items.title: 'Illegal, unauthorised': Election Commissioners objected to Form 6 change
items.shows: It is a companion piece, and it shows how a new declaration section was added to Form 6 against the written advice of two Commissioners, who said it needed an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules.

items.title: No VIP Left Behind: ECI’s Drive to Guarantee a Spot For Them on the Final Voter Roll
items.authors: Ayushi Kar, Shubhangi Derhgawen, Sumedha Mittal, Dikshya Koirala
items.shows: It reports that the Delhi revision gave people the Commission treated as VIPs a separate route onto the roll, through a 'Mark VIP' module in the booth-level officers' app, WhatsApp groups and orders. Ordinary electors with notices were sent to queues and hearings.

items.title: The Mysterious 16.18 Lakh Voters Added to Uttar Pradesh’s Roll
items.shows: It sets the 71.38 lakh Form 6 applications the Uttar Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer published against the 84.3 lakh electors added to the final roll. It traces the gap to 16.18 lakh applications taken before the draft, whose names and details were never published as the rules require.

items.title: UP CEO Confirms: 16.18 Lakh Applications for Addition Accepted Before Draft Roll. Falsely Claims Details Were Hidden on ECI’s Instructions
items.shows: It follows the earlier report on 16.18 lakh additions in Uttar Pradesh. The state's Chief Electoral Officer confirmed the Form 6 applications were taken before the draft roll and said their details were withheld on the Commission's instructions, and the report sets that against Commission instructions requiring applications after the draft and public details.

items.title: In UP SIR, ECI Software Auto-generated 85,854 Forms to Delete Voters Without a Reason
items.authors: Sumedha Mittal, Ayushi Kar, Shubhangi Derhgawen
items.shows: From the more than 4.3 lakh Form 7 objections the Uttar Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer published, it finds that the roll software generated 85,854 deletion forms giving no reason, carrying the officers' digital signatures. It also counts 1,10,476 deletion requests from individuals accepted after the legal deadline.

items.title: Delhi SIR: ECI Forcing BLOs to Sign Off on Voters Without Verification
items.shows: It reports that booth-level officers in Delhi were told over WhatsApp to clear electors flagged for 'logical discrepancies' by signing a new 'certificate' form. Under this route the flagged cases are closed with no documents and no hearing.

items.title: UP CEO Admits ECI Auto-generated 85,000+ Voter Deletion Forms Without a Reason, Confirms Mass Deletion Attempts Against Muslims
items.authors: Sumedha Mittal, Ayushi Kar (edited by Nitin Sethi)
items.shows: It is a follow-up to the Collective's investigation of 9 October 2026 into the 85,854 Form 7s that the Commission's software ERONET produced in Uttar Pradesh with no reason for deletion. It reports that the state's Chief Electoral Officer answered on X within minutes, calling the report false, and that evening called it misleading in a recorded video, in which he did not dispute the count or explain why the reasons were missing. It quotes him putting the names targeted by bulk Form 7s at about 4,700 among 13.39 crore electors, and reports that the Commission capped the number of deletion objections one person may file.

items.title: Amit Shah and ECI claim SIR Was to Catch ‘Infiltrators’. Commission Has no Record of Them
items.authors: Ayushi Kar (edited by Mayank Aggarwal, visual by Nitin Sethi)
items.shows: From its RTI applications and its reporting on the Commission's software, the Collective finds that the SIR gave officers no way to record anyone as a foreigner. The Commission passed its questions on cases referred under the Citizenship Act to Bihar alone. The Bihar replies it reproduces answer No to whether any list was referred and give the constituency's names left off by reason, with no category for people who are not citizens. It sets this beside the Home Minister's statement that the Leader of the Opposition was protecting infiltrators.

items.title: Inside India’s electoral overhaul that removed 130mn voters
items.shows: It reports from Hyderabad, where the revision was in its last phase, on residents of a Muslim neighbourhood whose names were left off the draft roll, one of whom said 17 members of his family and 13 neighbours were left off, his family as permanently shifted. It sets out critics' view that the revision wrongly took eligible voters off the rolls, many of them Muslim, and may have helped the Prime Minister's party, and notes that protesters have produced no evidence that it changed any result. It quotes a former election commissioner calling the exercise aggressive, ambitious and abrupt, and the Commission's reply that its decisions follow standard administrative practice and that it has directed officials to restore eligible voters left off in error. The 130 million in its headline are names left off the drafts.

items.title: The ECI Software Deleted 5.38 Lakh Bengal Voters With Auto-Generated Rejections Without Citing a Reason
items.shows: It reads the Form 10 registers published with West Bengal's final roll for 284 of the 294 constituencies and finds 5,23,998 names deleted on Form 7s that give the Electoral Registration Officer as the objector and leave the reason blank. It quotes the Chief Electoral Officer's statement of 6 March 2026 that the state's Form 7 figure included forms the Commission's software generated when an officer did not approve an elector at a hearing, and puts those at 5,38,320 of the state's 5.46 lakh Form 7 deletions. It breaks the deletions down by district and by the party that won each seat, and sets them against the 2026 margins.

items.title: Audit finds Bengal-specific access curbs in ECINET code
items.shows: It reports a review of ECINET's publicly served code by Saurav Rajput, a data scientist at the civic-tech initiative Charchagram, which found a rule that can bar registration officers in West Bengal from the page that shows each enumeration form with its documents and from the notice-and-hearing dashboard, and found no such rule for any other state. The review read only the code a browser receives before login, so it cannot say whether the rule was used or enforced on the server, and the paper says it could not verify the review. The Commission did not answer the paper's questions.

items.title: On ECINet platform, access for States can be switched off and on centrally: report
items.shows: It reports another finding from Saurav Rajput's review of ECINET's code for the civic-tech initiative Charchagram. The portal has an area for managing State Nodal Officers with a disable button on each, and the code carries a message for States where viewing enumeration form details is not enabled. The review read only code the site serves before login, and the report does not say who can use either control or whether either was used.

items.title: ECINET Audit Finds State-Level Access Could be Restricted by Election Commission, VIP Tags for Voters
items.shows: It is Saurav Rajput's review of ECINET's publicly served code for the civic-tech initiative Charchagram, reported in three findings. Besides the State Nodal Officer controls and the West Bengal rule, it reports code showing a gold VIP symbol against some voters on officials' screens and a button that downloads a list of these voters by constituency. The review cannot say whether any feature was used, and the criteria for marking a voter are not known.

items.title: The Election Commission Filed 16 Lakh Appeals Against Included Bengal Voters Over Just 3 Days as the Rolls Froze
items.shows: The appeal records for West Bengal, collected by the Civic Research Group and checked by The Wire, show the Commission appealed against 16,08,175 of the 32,53,401 voters the judicial officers had cleared, or 49.4%. In an earlier extract of 13,95,794 appeal IDs, 99.3% carry a timestamp of 5, 6 or 8 April, and more than 12 lakh carry 5 April. The Commission told the Supreme Court in September that it had filed 16,10,311 appeals against inclusion.

items.title: Uttarakhand ERO refused BJP worker’s bulk Form 7 objections. After ECI complaint, 5,359 were accepted
items.shows: It follows the Form 7 objections in Kichha, Uttarakhand, from the Chief Electoral Officer's Form 10 data to the final roll of 3 October. Of 4,390 names on the draft that are missing from the final roll, about 670 had an objection against them and 3,720 had none and were deleted for logical discrepancies. One BJP booth level agent filed 5,359 of the 6,884 objections accepted, and 504 of his carry an acceptance date a day after claims closed. A second part meets electors deleted after his objections whose notices gave other reasons.

items.title: यूपी में एसआईआर की जिन गड़बड़ियों को लेकर चुनाव आयोग है निशाने पर
items.shows: It sets out what is known of the Pilibhit Sadar case, from the Congress's allegation of 13,150 changed names to the Chief Electoral Officer's note of 22 October on 13,779 Form 8 entries with no records behind them. BBC Hindi checked rolls itself and found two electors at one polling station in Bareilly each entered under two EPIC numbers, and one elector in Pilibhit Sadar entered under three. It could not reach Pilibhit's Deputy District Election Officer for comment. It also recounts the Samajwadi Party's complaint of duplicates and the Chief Electoral Officer's instruction of 19 October to delete them through Form 7.

items.title: 'Dear Bengal Poll Chief, How Many Voters Have ECI Staff Tried to Delete?' Asks Jawhar Sircar
items.shows: It reports the nine questions that Jawhar Sircar, a former Rajya Sabha member and former Secretary to the Government of India, put in a letter to West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer, Neelam Meena. He asks how many applications election officers filed before the tribunals to delete names, under what authority and how many names were deleted, which notification introduced 'logical discrepancies' and how many electors they affected, whether ECINET can stop registration officers from seeing enumeration forms and the hearing dashboard, and whether every elector left off is covered by the special drive. The report sets the questions beside its own earlier figures on the appeals and the discrepancy flags.

items.title: Over 61,000 Form-7 applications filed by election officials in Karnataka, none cites reason
items.shows: It counts 61,059 Form 7 applications in Karnataka filed by registration officers themselves, none giving a reason, from the Commission's Form 10 records, and finds that more than 60,800 of them came after claims closed on 23 September. Officers said the system generated the forms with their digital signatures when electors sent notices could not be reached. Every elector the paper checked had already been deleted, and in at least 26 constituencies officers filed more objections than voters or third parties did.

items.title: On last day of SIR camps in Delhi, BLOs wait, go door to door
items.shows: It visits the special enrolment camps in Chilla, New Moti Bagh and Sarai Kale Khan on their last day, where booth level officers received few or no Form 6 applications and spent the day on notices and door to door visits. It sets this against about 47.5 lakh electors left off Delhi's draft of 31 August and about 4.7 lakh Form 6 applications so far, and follows a first time applicant held up at the declaration about his parents' entry in the last intensive revision.

items.title: Election Commission's SIR exercise identifies just 1,600 foreigners on voter lists in six states
items.shows: Hindustan Times reports that it approached the Chief Electoral Officers of 26 states and union territories where the revision was complete or a draft roll had been published, and that officials in 11 of them answered. Six gave a count of suspected foreign nationals, about 1,600 in all among some 9.86 crore electors. By the paper's account they were 716 in Karnataka, about 500 in Kerala, 419 suspected foreign passport holders in Goa, three in Jharkhand, two in Meghalaya and none in Mizoram. Officials in Punjab, Delhi, Uttarakhand and Telangana said they kept no such figure, and an official in Odisha said cases were found and not counted. The paper quotes a senior official of the Commission saying that states were not asked to collect the figure separately and that such cases went under the category Others. It sets these counts beside the Commission's press note of 24 June 2025, which named the inclusion of foreign illegal immigrants among the reasons for the revision.

items.title: ECI’s Software and Rules Allow the Pilibhit Fake-Voter Playbook to Run Anywhere in India
items.authors: Ayushi Kar, Shubhangi Derhgawen, Sumedha Mittal, Dikshya Koirala (edited by Nitin Sethi)
items.shows: From the Commission's own roll data for 55 of Pilibhit's 419 booths, matched by EPIC number against the final roll of 10 April 2026, the Collective finds 2,691 entries whose names were replaced after the SIR, most of them in August, and 2,638 of them still on the roll eight days after the Chief Electoral Officer's finding on the Form 8 entries. From the Commission's Form 8 manual and the code of the ECINET and ERONET apps, it reports that a registration officer can start a correction, pass over the booth level officer's field check and approve it, that the software does not require supporting documents to be uploaded, and that the published correction forms carry no EPIC number, so the public has no reliable way to tell which entries changed. It argues that the same rules and software apply in every state.

items.title: A Chinese state group backdoored ArcGIS for a year. It is now being used for Census 2027.
items.shows: From the bid papers on GeM, the Internet Freedom Foundation reports that the Office of the Registrar General bought 96 Esri ArcGIS licences for Census 2027 under a Proprietary Article Certificate, which rules out competition on the product, on a file numbered XII-027/23/2019-MAP and carried forward from 2019. It reports that the contract went on 10 June 2026 to Corporate Infotech Private Limited for ₹14,38,74,322, after four resellers of the same Esri India product bid within 0.95 per cent of each other in a reverse auction, and that its scope covers the Houselisting Block Creator, the Census Thematic Mapper and the Digital District Census Hand Book in every state and union territory. Citing a ReliaQuest report of October 2025, IFF says a group that ReliaQuest assessed with moderate confidence to be the Chinese state-sponsored Flax Typhoon kept a backdoor in an unnamed organisation's ArcGIS Server for over a year, and that Esri put the compromise down to the victim's configuration and issued no patch. IFF notes that the work in the bid covers boundaries, maps and tabulated data and does not route individual records or caste answers through Esri's software directly. It finds no public record of a security audit, of CERT-In clearance or of the reasons for passing over Bhuvan and open-source tools, and it has filed RTI applications. The piece concerns the Census mapping software and says nothing about the electoral rolls, the SIR or the National Population Register.

items.title: Telangana SIR: How 73 Lakh Voters Were Marked for Deletion
items.shows: Frontline follows how electors in Hyderabad came to be left off Telangana's draft roll, from public data and interviews with electors, the Chief Electoral Officer, registration officers, booth level officers and party agents. It gives the 73,39,235 names left off a roll of about 3.38 crore by reason, 9,22,229 dead, 11,25,546 untraceable or absent, 45,18,963 permanently shifted, 6,70,203 already enrolled and 1,02,294 others. It reports that the SIR guidelines let a booth level officer note a probable cause for an elector whose form did not come back, and two booth level officers told the magazine that they marked everyone who did not come to the community centre as having refused the form, whether or not they had refused it. In Chandrayangutta the tentative list of names to be left off grew from 37,241 on 29 July to 1,48,869 on 11 August, and the registration officer told the magazine that names were marked on the last day. In Bahadurpura such names rose from 40,038 on 3 August to 1,21,350 at the draft. Matching the Form 9 reports of Form 6 applications that the Chief Electoral Officer published for 13 of Hyderabad's 15 seats against the names left off, by name and relation's name, it counts 2,561 electors left off who applied on Form 6, and calls the figure indicative. It also gives the Chief Electoral Officer's figures of 4,88,417 Form 6 applications in the state from 15 June to 7 October, of which about 51,821 had been added by 8 October.

items.title: Deleted from India's voter rolls, some Muslims face detention, deportation
items.authors: Sarita Chaganti Singh, Mohammad Ponir Hossain (Reuters)
items.shows: Reuters reports that India's revision of the rolls left off or deleted 130 million names, and it says data shows the omissions fall disproportionately on Muslims. It spoke to 10 families whose relatives were detained, deported or questioned about their citizenship after their names were dropped from the rolls, and it says all of them had Indian identity or family documents while relatives, among them parents and siblings, stayed on the rolls. It reports that a woman from West Bengal, on the state's rolls since at least 2008 by the voter card Reuters saw, says she was detained in Mumbai on 19 July and forced across the border into Bangladesh, and that court filings show she was one of 149 people deported in that operation. It reports that Mumbai's Foreigners Regional Registration Office told the Calcutta High Court she had produced a Bangladeshi birth certificate and no valid or credible documentary evidence of Indian citizenship, and that she disputes this. It reports a petition in the Calcutta High Court by five people who say they were detained after their names were deleted from the rolls while their appeals were pending before the special tribunals. One of them told Reuters that police in Chhattisgarh detained him with 22 others, that 19 were released after 14 days when their names were found on the revised rolls, and that he and three others were held for 32 days. It cites the Sabar Institute for the finding that Muslims were about 70% of the 2.7 million names deleted in West Bengal after a closer review, against 27% of the population. It quotes Home Minister Amit Shah at a rally in Haryana on 5 November saying that the BJP would detect infiltrators, remove them from the rolls and expel them. It says that removal from the roll does not by itself establish that anyone is a foreigner, and that the Home Ministry, the Prime Minister's Office and the Election Commission did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: In Jharkhand’s SIR, Everyone Who Gets a Notice Pays For it
items.shows: A research intern with Jean Dreze reports from the hearings at the Ranchi collectorate on 2 September, from two booth level officers, one at a booth in urban Ranchi and one at a rural booth in Bagodar, and from the published lists of unmapped electors for two booths in Hatia. He reports that people who came with only a voter ID card and Aadhaar were asked for a caste or residence certificate, and that stalls outside drew up affidavits for Rs 300 to Rs 500 each, though as far as he could tell most were not needed. He puts the minimum wage for unskilled work in Jharkhand's larger cities at about Rs 520 a day, so that an affidavit can cost most of a day's pay. He reports that about two in five of the 172 unmapped electors on the two Hatia lists are women recorded only through a husband's name, and that over half of them are 41 or older. The booth level officers name migrant workers, women who cannot produce a parent's entry and tenants in urban areas as the electors most easily lost, and he reports that many elderly electors who received notices cannot keep travelling to the office. One of the officers describes an Election Commission portal whose server often goes down. He cites the Chief Electoral Officer's office for 63,24,116 electors on the draft roll to be served notices, and for Hatia as the constituency with the most notices, 1,52,362. He says the account rests on two booths, two booth level officers and one visit, and makes no claim beyond them.

items.title: Bengal faces fresh electoral roll revision amid 21 lakh pending SIR deletion appeals
items.shows: The Federal reports that West Bengal's summary revision, with its draft due on 23 November and its final roll on 16 January 2027, begins while appeals against deletions after the adjudication of logical discrepancies are still pending before the appellate tribunals, more than 21.7 lakh of them by its count. It cites the Civic Research Group's analysis of the Commission's data and tribunal records for more than 27 lakh electors deleted after adjudication, with nearly 21 lakh of those who appealed still awaiting a decision. It reports that estimates from different sets of records put the electors still marked under adjudication, with no final order they could appeal, at around 30,000, and sets that against the Chief Electoral Officer's office's count of 815 undecided cases and 5,004 decisions awaiting e-signatures. It reports that booth level officers have been asked to visit electors who were on the rolls before the revision and are missing now, and to help those eligible apply on Form 6. The general secretary of an association of booth level officers said they had not been told to use a new facility in the BLO app for uploading documents in tribunal cases. The paper reports from party sources that a BJP team of about 200 leaders will visit all 294 Assembly constituencies from 26 November to record views on the revision.

items.title: In 200 Seats, the ECI Has No Record of How Many Citizens Voted After 5 PM in 2024 Elections
items.shows: It concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In Part 2 of its Election Audit series, the Reporters' Collective reports that it read the Election Commission's internal reports of the returning officers for 530 Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir that voted in 2024, and that in 200 of them the reports carry no count of votes polled after 5 pm. It gives these as 114 of Maharashtra's 288 Assembly seats, 44 of Jammu and Kashmir's 90 and 22 of Haryana's 90, with 18 of Maharashtra's 48 Lok Sabha seats and one each in Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir. It says the Commission's rules require the presiding officer to note the votes on the machine every two hours and tally them against the register of voters, and that in 23 seats the number of slips handed to voters still in the queue at the close of poll was not recorded. In the 174 Maharashtra Assembly seats where the count was recorded, it finds 50.87 lakh votes cast after 5 pm. It says it does not conclude whether or where voting was rigged. The Chief Electoral Officers of Haryana, Jammu and Kashmir and Maharashtra answered on X on 18 November that the Commission publishes the votes polled in its index cards, that Form 17C is the statutory account given to the polling agents at the close of poll, that the returning officer's report is a non-statutory summary, and that no separate statutory record of polling after 5 pm exists. In a thread on 19 November one of the reporters, Sumedha Mittal, called that answer misleading and said the missing figures are the two-hourly counts from the presiding officer's diary, which reach the Commission's headquarters through the returning officer's report.

items.title: For N Chandrababu Naidu’s 2024 Win, the ECI Recorded an Impossibility After 6 PM. Then Did Not Investigate
items.shows: It concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In Part 3 of its Election Audit series, the Reporters' Collective reports that two returning officers' reports sent to the Commission a day apart give different counts of voters still in the queue at 6 pm in Chittoor in Andhra Pradesh, where the Lok Sabha and Assembly polls were held together at the same booths. It says the report for the Chittoor Lok Sabha seat counted 56,067 such voters and the report for the seven Assembly seats that make up Chittoor counted 24,596, a gap of more than 31,000, and that the Commission never looked into it. It explains that the presiding officer hands numbered slips to the voters in the queue at the close of poll and records the number issued in the diary, which the returning officer scrutinises the next day. It notes that N. Chandrababu Naidu of the Telugu Desam Party won Kuppam, one of the seven Assembly seats, and became Chief Minister, and that the party won the Lok Sabha seat and all seven Assembly seats. The Collective says it has so far reviewed the returning officers' reports for only one parliamentary seat, that the Commission did not answer its questions, and that the Chief Electoral Officer's office referred it to the district election officer.

items.title: Maharashtra CEO Responds: Two Truths in Two Records
items.shows: This reply concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In a blog post of 24 November signed by its editors, the Reporters' Collective answers the letter of 20 November in which the office of Maharashtra's Chief Electoral Officer called misleading its report that the Commission has no record of how many citizens voted after 5 pm in the 2024 elections. The Collective says it stands by its reporting and that the Chief Electoral Officer has not disputed that the internal reports it cites exist or what they contain. It says all reports the Commission and its officials produce should reflect the same data, that the internal reports it read are prescribed by the Commission's manuals, are mandatory and are sent to the Commission in sealed envelopes, and that the manual says any difference between the count of voters who polled and the votes counted should be investigated as a case of potential rigging. It says the manual requires officials to record the voters and the votes polled every two hours until polling ends, and that filling in these figures after polling is over defeats the purpose of an audit. On the letter's complaint that questions sent at 10.03 am on 16 November asked for a reply by 5 pm that day, the Collective says it gave adequate time, that the office neither replied nor asked for more time, and that the questions needed no check of older records.

items.title: Press Note: Special Intensive Revision - Phase III (No. ECI/PN/086/2026)
items.shows: It is the Commission's own announcement of the third phase in 16 states and 3 union territories, with its count of booth level officers and agents and its summary of the first two phases.

items.title: 'Differing views' part of 'decision-making', says EC, does not address concerns two ECs red-flagged
items.shows: It reports the Election Commission's first response to the investigation. The Commission calls the 14 notes suggestions and says every decision was unanimous, and the paper sets out what the response does not address.

items.title: Press Note (No. ECI/PN/120/2026): decisions of the meeting of the Commission held on 26.09.2026
items.shows: It finds that the 17 phase 3 states and territories with draft rolls left off 6.15 crore names, 17.1%, against 12.3% in the first two phases, with a larger share marked shifted or absent. It also finds that the full lists of names left off for Delhi, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Telangana mark no one as 'Others', though the Chief Electoral Officers' press notes put 9.73 lakh names left off in phase 3 under that reason.

items.title: Press Note (No. ECI/PN/121/2026)
items.shows: It records a Commission meeting attended by all three Commissioners that extended the SIR in Andhra Pradesh (claims and notices to 10 October, final roll on 16 October) and moved Meghalaya's final roll to 26 October 2026.

items.title: Special drive in States/UTs after completion of Special Intensive Revision (SIR) – reg. (Letter No. 23/2025/ERS(Vol-II))
items.shows: It is the Commission's letter to all Chief Electoral Officers ordering a drive to enrol left-out and young electors. Booth-level officers are to compare the current roll with the pre-SIR roll, list everyone missing, visit each house within about a month, help eligible people fill Form 6 and share the lists with party agents.

items.title: Factual Position regarding report published on reporters-collective.in
items.shows: It concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In a four-page note posted on 18 November, in reply to the Reporters' Collective's report that the returning officers' reports for 200 seats in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir carry no count of votes polled after 5 pm, the Chief Electoral Officer of Haryana says that the Commission publishes the electors, the votes polled on the machines and by post and the turnout of every seat in its index cards, which are generated by the system from the records made at polling and counting. It says the presiding officer records the total of votes polled in Form 17C at the close of poll and gives a copy to every polling agent present. It describes the returning officer's report as an administrative narrative of the conduct of the poll, drawn from the presiding officer's diary and other papers, filled in by hand and non-statutory, and says that a divergence between the two is a difference in the design of the two reporting formats and no evidence of wrongdoing. It says no separate statutory record of polling after 5 pm exists, that the final figure is recorded at the close of poll and at no fixed clock time, and that the register of voters, the presiding officer's diary and other papers are scrutinised on the day after the poll so that a repoll can be recommended where needed. The Chief Electoral Officer of Jammu and Kashmir posted the first six points the same day on a card that calls the report misleading. In a thread on 19 November one of the Collective's reporters, Sumedha Mittal, called the reply misleading and said the missing figures are the two-hourly counts from the presiding officer's diary, which reach the Commission's headquarters through the returning officer's report.

items.title: Reply of the Chief Electoral Officer, Maharashtra, to The Reporters’ Collective
items.shows: This letter concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In a four-page letter to the Reporters' Collective dated 20 November and posted on X on 22 November, signed by M.R. Parkar, Joint Secretary and Joint Chief Electoral Officer, the office of Maharashtra's Chief Electoral Officer says the Collective's report is based on factual inaccuracies and calls its title completely misleading. It says that at the Assembly election of 2024 the returning officers entered the polling percentage every two hours in the Commission's Encore software from the start of the poll, that citizens could see it on the Voter Turnout app for each slot from 7 am to 5 pm, and that after this an approximate percentage at the close of poll was made available and finally what it calls the accurate percentage, collected from the presiding officers, was published on the same app. It says the hours of poll were 7 am to 6 pm in 285 of the 288 Assembly seats and were cut to 3 pm in three seats of Gadchiroli district, and on its third page it gives the hours of 7 am to 6 pm for 283 of the 288. It describes the returning officer's report in Annexure 44 as an administrative narrative of 48 points written by hand and a non-statutory summary, and says the figures in the Commission's index cards trace back to Form 17C. It says the Collective's statement that officials kept no record of voting between 5 pm and 6 pm in 114 Assembly seats rests on point 42 of that report, which asks only for the votes cast every two hours up to 5 pm and the slips issued at the close of poll, and that the votes cast after 5 pm in any seat can be worked out by subtracting the votes at 5 pm from the total recorded at point 18. It says the number of slips handed to voters in the queue at the close of poll is recorded in the presiding officer's diary, which it calls a statutory document. It gives the turnout at the Assembly election of 2024 as 58.22% at 5 pm and 66.05% at the end of poll, a difference of 7.83, against 6.67 at the Assembly election of 2019 and between 8.23 and 10.15 in the five phases of the Lok Sabha election of 2024 in the state, and says the voting shows no surge after 5 pm. It says the Collective emailed its questions on 16 November at 10.03 am and asked for a reply by 5 pm the same day.

items.title: SIR Row: Seven fake claims made on electoral roll by Congress and opposition examined and debunked
items.shows: Organiser sets out the BJP's account of the revision, from a video the party posted on 25 October 2026 in answer to seven allegations by the INDIA bloc. By the BJP's account, the 13 crore names were only flagged in the drafts as dead, shifted, absent or duplicate, Form 6 itself is unchanged and the Supreme Court upheld the declaration added to it, registration officers in each state still manage the rolls, and about 2.37 crore young electors have been added since the revision began. The BJP also says the three Election Commissioners decide together, lists five safeguards against fraud and defends the 2023 law on appointing them. Organiser adds that these figures need checking against official records. On 12 October 2026 the Supreme Court said it had neither approved nor disapproved the modified Form 6, as Bar and Bench reported. In its affidavit of 26 October 2026 the Commission told the Supreme Court that Form 6 had not been amended and that the declaration is a separate document, as Bar and Bench reported.

items.title: ECI affidavit on SIR is ‘deceitful and duplicitous’: Congress
items.shows: The Hindu reports the Congress's answer to the Election Commission's affidavit of 26 October 2026 in the Supreme Court. Jairam Ramesh, the party's general secretary for communications, called the 248-page counter-affidavit deceptive, deceitful and duplicitous. He said the Commission had first claimed the Supreme Court upheld the declaration attached to Form 6 and now says the declaration is separate and Form 6 was not amended, while an online Form 6 could not be submitted without it. He also said the two Election Commissioners had recorded objections that were disregarded and that ECINet was used to override electoral registration officers. Party president Mallikarjun Kharge posted a graphic of alleged irregularities from 12 states and one union territory and asked why the Prime Minister and the Home Minister were protecting the Chief Election Commissioner. By The Hindu's account the Commission has said its SIR orders were issued under Article 324 and the law governing it.

items.title: Pawan Khera on the Commission's affidavit and Instagram
items.shows: Pawan Khera of the Congress says the Commission's affidavit is riddled with inconsistencies and contradictions, and alleges that the government asked Meta to have copies of the affidavit and explanations of it taken down from Instagram. He names no post. Earlier the same day LiveLaw reported that Instagram had blocked for users in India its reel explaining the Commission's affidavit, with the message "We received a legal request to restrict this content". At 10:21 pm IST LiveLaw said Instagram had restored the video. Neither LiveLaw nor Instagram said who made the request. No statement from Meta, the government or the Commission on the request was found.

items.title: Who is being left out of voter rolls? What Aadhaar reveals about SIR
items.shows: Praveen Chakravarty, a Congress Member of Parliament and chairperson of the party's data analytics department, sets the count of adults with Aadhaar from UIDAI's saturation report against the rolls after the revision in 14 states. By his count 9 crore adults with Aadhaar in the 14 states are not on the rolls. In Uttar Pradesh he gives 16.3 crore adults with Aadhaar against 13.4 crore electors on the final roll, and puts the gap at 2.5 to 3 crore after allowing for deaths, people abroad and foreign citizens. He gives the gap as 21 per cent of adults in Goa, 19 per cent in Punjab and Uttarakhand and 7 per cent in Odisha and Tamil Nadu. He argues that migration cannot explain it, because no state that receives migrants has more electors than adults with Aadhaar and Bihar has one of the smallest gaps, and he replies to Surjit Bhalla's argument that the gap is adults who did not register. The column does not print the figures for each state.

items.title: Migrants and a maze of deletions
items.shows: Manish Tewari, a Lok Sabha MP of the Congress and a former Minister of Information and Broadcasting, argues that the map of names left off the drafts follows the map of India's internal migration. He takes his figures on migration from the National Sample Survey Office's Multiple Indicator Survey of 2020-21. By his account about 26.8 per cent of people in rural areas and 34.6 per cent in urban areas lived somewhere other than their usual place of residence, and 87.2 per cent of those who moved stayed within their state. Of those who moved, 93.4 per cent of women in rural areas and 71.5 per cent in urban areas moved after marriage, and 38.7 per cent of men in rural areas and 56.1 per cent in urban areas moved for work. He says Delhi draws 64.7 per cent of its urban migrants and 64 per cent of its rural ones from other states, and that there are about 23 migrant workers for every 100 urban men in Telangana, 18 in Maharashtra, 17 in Delhi, 5 in Bihar and fewer than 8 in Uttar Pradesh. Across 18 sets of rolls he finds that the share of names left off the draft correlates at 0.50 with the survey's measure of urban work migration and at 0.56 with net migration from the Census, and he finds almost no relationship with the overall migration rate that includes moves for marriage. Where the reasons are split he puts deaths at 1.5 to 4.2 per cent of each state's roll, and electors marked shifted or absent at 4.3 per cent in West Bengal and 29.9 per cent in Delhi. He names Uttar Pradesh, a large sender of labour that marked 14.06 per cent of its electors shifted or absent, and Odisha, which he says has a high count of urban work migrants and the lowest share left off, as exceptions. He argues that the revision has no way of telling that a name deleted in one state is still on the roll in another, and calls for it to be scrapped, for the rolls of 4 June 2024 to be restored and for continuous registration that a voter can carry from place to place.

items.title: 'SIR Risks Disenfranchising Millions of Legitimate Citizens Over Lack of Documents': Lokniti-CSDS Survey
items.shows: It reports a Lokniti-CSDS survey across Delhi and five states. 52% of respondents had no birth certificate and 41% no domicile certificate, with sharp gaps between states.

items.title: Bihar SIR: Latest ECI data raises more questions over higher deletions among women
items.authors: Areena Arora, Srinivasan Ramani, Vignesh Radhakrishnan
items.shows: Using the list of about 65 lakh Bihar electors left off the draft, which the Supreme Court made the Commission publish, it shows women far outnumbered men among those marked 'permanently shifted', most of all below age 40.

items.title: More men die in Bihar, but more women vanish from its voter rolls
items.shows: It sets the Commission's counts of names left off by reason and sex against state death records and finds about 7.6 lakh more women than men left off, including more women entered as dead, although more men die.

items.title: Why exclusion of women voters in Bihar should worry Nitish Kumar
items.shows: It compares Bihar's January 2025 roll with the final SIR roll and finds women were close to 59% of the fall in the roll and the gender ratio of the roll fell in 230 of 243 seats.

items.title: Bihar 2025: In 11 Seats, SIR Deletions Outnumbered Victory Margins
items.shows: It finds 11 Bihar seats where the names left off or deleted exceeded the winning margin, separates the 47 lakh net fall from the 3.66 lakh deleted after the draft, and says the landslide made the numbers moot statewide.

items.title: What Election Commission data says about 'vote chori' in the Bihar elections
items.shows: It checks booth-level results in villages where many names were left off or deleted, the 28 close contests and late additions to the roll, and finds no anomaly that stands out. The NDA won exactly half the close contests.

items.title: After SIR, 13.4% deletions in Gujarat electoral rolls
items.authors: Abhishek Jha, Maulik Pathak, Harsh Yadav
items.shows: It reads Gujarat's final roll of 4.40 crore against the pre-SIR roll, a net fall of 13.4 per cent. The largest falls were in Surat, Ahmedabad and Vadodara and the smallest in the tribal districts of Dang, Chhota Udepur and Narmada.

items.title: Bengal Has 62 Lakh 'Under Adjudication' Electors. Here's Why That Number Is Significant.
items.shows: It sets West Bengal's final roll against the National Commission on Population's projection of adults for 2026 and finds a gap of about 65.7 lakh, with electors at about 91.5% of projected adults.

items.title: More women deleted from rolls in most States after SIR
items.shows: It compares women per 1,000 men on the 2024 Lok Sabha rolls and the final SIR rolls across the second-phase states and finds the ratio fell in every major state except Tamil Nadu.

items.title: Over 61 Lakh Women Dropped from Bengal Voter Rolls, Data Show Stark Gender Bias in SIR
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Ashin Chakraborty, Bhanupriya Rao, Souptik Halder
items.shows: From the Commission's lists, it finds roughly three in five electors left off, deleted or held under adjudication on West Bengal's roll were women, most heavily in Muslim-majority, Scheduled Tribe and Matua seats.

items.title: 4 tests, 1 question: Did SIR shape Bengal outcome?
items.shows: It runs four tests of the names West Bengal left off or deleted against the 2026 margins and swings. The net count exceeded the BJP's margin in 82 seats but exceeded the swing in margin in only 12 flipped seats, and the names held for adjudication passed the two tests in 49 and 14 seats.

items.title: SIR redraws Bengal’s margins of power
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Ashin Chakraborty, Souptik Halder
items.shows: It finds the names left off or deleted in West Bengal's revision outnumbered the winning margin in 161 of 293 Assembly seats, and still did so in 124 seats once deaths are left out.

items.title: SIR exclusions in West Bengal were connected to the AITC lead and Muslim population
items.shows: Using the Sabar Institute's data on names left off or deleted, it reports that those names exceeded the margin in 102 of the BJP's 207 seats and, by its own summary, a regression in which they rose with how hard a seat was for the BJP to win.

items.title: Data analysis: How SIR deletions shaped BJP’s landslide in Bengal
items.shows: It sets each West Bengal seat's roll shrinkage against the change in the BJP and TMC margin from 2021 to 2026, and finds each point of shrinkage went with a shift of about 0.38 points toward the BJP. The same test on Bihar finds no such pattern, and the authors describe the Bengal result as an association.

items.title: Comprehensive Analysis of ASDD Deletions in Uttarakhand under the Special Intensive Revision of Electoral Rolls, 2026
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Souptik Halder, Ashin Chakraborty
items.shows: It finds at least 8,07,410 names on Uttarakhand's ASDD lists, 52.0% of them women and 57.7% recorded as permanently shifted, more than the 2022 winning margin in 45 of 70 seats.

items.title: Fact Sheet on Voter Deletion Patterns in the West Bengal Special Intensive Revision (SIR), 2025–26
items.shows: Reading 91 lakh elector records, it finds women were 53.6% of the 58 lakh names left off the draft in December 2025 and that in Nandigram, where Muslims are about a quarter of the population, they were 95% of the names deleted from the supplementary lists.

items.title: Preliminary Report on SIR Meghalaya : State-wide analysis of all 60 Assembly Constituencies
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Souptik Halder, Ashin Chakraborty
items.shows: It finds 1,80,402 names on Meghalaya's ASDD lists, 8.32% of the draft roll, with death the largest recorded reason at 45.2% and the count above the 2023 winning margin in 32 of 60 seats.

items.title: Bengaluru to Lucknow, why urban centres are seeing high electoral roll deletions during SIR
items.shows: It compares the district with the highest share of names left off in several states, which are the Bengaluru districts in Karnataka (43 to 49 per cent), Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh, Surat in Gujarat, Chennai in Tamil Nadu, Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh, Gurugram and Hyderabad. A former Chief Election Commissioner and a former Election Commissioner put the pattern down to migration, and the second says that deleting electors for failing to map to the 2002-03 roll would be unfair.

items.title: SIR draft rolls see over 13 crore deletions so far, Delhi leads with 33% left out
items.shows: It tallies the names left off the draft rolls across the states revised so far, over 13 crore, with Delhi the highest at about a third of its roll.

items.title: SIR Draft Rolls Show Highest Voter Deletions in States Where Elections Were Held in Last 3 Years
items.shows: It tabulates the phase 3 draft rolls, 6.15 crore names left off across 17 states and UTs. The five states with the most names left off (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Delhi, Andhra Pradesh) all held Assembly elections between 2023 and 2025, and the lowest shares were in Mizoram, Odisha, Manipur, Meghalaya and Sikkim.

items.title: SIR Delhi 2026: The Excluded Roll and the 2025 Verdict
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Souptik Halder, Ashin Chakraborty
items.shows: Across all 14,947 polling parts it counts 47,56,722 uncollectable enumeration forms, 32.8% of Delhi's electorate, more than the 2025 winning margin in 68 of 70 seats.

items.title: SIR: Glaring oddities in Maharashtra’s deletion patterns
items.shows: It finds that shifted or absent made up 75% to 96.5% of the deletions in 85 Maharashtra constituencies, and that neighbouring seats in Pune used the two reasons very differently. It estimates that the draft roll falls about 1.92 crore short of the projected adult population.

items.title: SIR: Deletions go up in Phase 3 with more marked as ‘Shifted’ or ‘Absent’
items.shows: It finds that shifted or absent made up 75% to 96.5% of the names left off in 85 Maharashtra constituencies, and that neighbouring seats in Pune used the two reasons very differently. It estimates that the draft roll falls about 1.92 crore short of the projected adult population.

items.title: In seat Kejriwal lost by thin margin, nearly 40% names added before 2025 polls missing in SIR draft
items.shows: It follows the New Delhi seat, which had 1,08,788 electors at the 2025 election and lost 37,315 names in the SIR draft. It finds that 560 of the 1,430 voters added in January 2025, about four in ten, are missing from the draft.

items.title: Telangana SIR: Who Is Missing From the Draft Rolls?
items.shows: Frontline reports a preliminary analysis that the Sabar Institute shared with it, of the names left off Telangana's draft roll in the 104 Assembly seats outside Hyderabad. Sabar compiled the Election Commission's booth-wise lists of absent, shifted, dead and duplicate electors and counted 53,96,806 names against the Commission's 53,97,791, and its total matched the Commission's in 31 of 32 districts. By its count about 50.2 per cent of the names are women's, and more women than men were left off in 91 of the 104 seats. It describes about 71 per cent of those women as married, with an average age of about 45. The roll has no column for marital status, and the article does not say how Sabar worked it out. It counts 1,152 third gender electors among the names left off, and Frontline gives 2,350 on Telangana's 2023 roll. It puts 85.8 per cent of the names, 46.31 lakh, as marked shifted, untraceable or already enrolled elsewhere. The roll has no column for religion either, and Sabar classifies the names by religion itself, counting a name as Muslim only where both the Telugu and the English spelling on the roll point to it. By that classification Muslim names are 12.5 per cent of the names left off, in districts where the 2011 Census puts Muslims at 8.8 per cent. In the seven seats the BJP won in 2023 they are, by the same classification, nearly 45 per cent of the names marked untraceable and 17 per cent of those marked dead. Sabar's lead researcher, Sabir Ahamed, tells Frontline that these figures show an association with religion, gender and other characteristics and cannot show that any of them caused a name to be left off. Sabar also finds 202 booths where more than 90 per cent of the names left off are Muslim names by its classification, and Sabir Ahamed says such a booth partly reflects who lives on that street and that only a check of the addresses on the ground can show why so many were marked untraceable. Of 532 booths it examined for the reasons recorded, it finds 512 where more than 95 per cent of the names left off carry the same reason, permanently shifted.

items.title: Explainer: Why fewer voters were deleted in Odisha compared to several other states
items.shows: It sets Odisha's net fall of 17.67 lakh (about 5.3 per cent) from the pre-SIR roll to the final roll of 21 September against other states. It gives a 94 per cent return of enumeration forms, few duplicates and mostly seasonal migration as the reasons, and explains how a deleted elector can appeal or reapply.

items.title: SIR Manipur 2026: Preliminary Report on Electoral Roll Deletions
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Souptik Halder, Ashin Chakraborty
items.shows: Of the 1,58,677 names left off the draft in Manipur, the 20 hill seats account for 66.4% and women for 55.96%, and women are the majority of those left off in all 60 seats.

items.title: Analysis and Explainer on How the SIR Excluded Voters at Scale
items.shows: It draws on official figures for names left off and an RTI reply on West Bengal appeals. Delhi's draft excluded 32.78% of electors, 91.13% of the decided West Bengal appeals restored the elector, and the public still cannot check the rolls.

items.title: SIR: Telangana may witness net deletion of 70 lakh names or more from electoral rolls
items.shows: It reports that Telangana's draft of 17 August left off more than 73 lakh electors while fresh enrolment applications stayed under 5 lakh, so the net fall may reach 70 lakh. The Chief Electoral Officer's figures show more than 10.2 lakh claims and objections received by 7 October.

items.title: The Link Between TCS, SIR’s Digital Stack, and the Noel Tata-N. Chandrasekaran Tussle
items.shows: It argues that ERONET and ECINET, the roll software Tata Consultancy Services built for the Commission, moved control of the roll away from the registration officers the law names, citing Goa's 97 electors and Uttar Pradesh's Form 7s. It says the links it draws to the Tata group prove no wrongdoing.

items.title: Amid elector apathy, EC extends Maharashtra SIR deadline yet again till October 26
items.shows: It gives the reasons behind Maharashtra's 2.07 crore names left off the draft (7.68 million shifted, 7.55 million absent, 3.48 million dead, 1.76 million duplicates). By 12 October only 8.33 lakh applications and 25,661 Form 7 objections had come in, and 1.22 crore electors on the draft were flagged as unmapped or discrepant.

items.title: Muslims disproportionately flagged in Delhi SIR
items.shows: The Hindu read Delhi's draft roll of 97.54 lakh electors, matched it to the lists of the 33.12 lakh sent notices (13.79 lakh unmapped with the last SIR and 19.33 lakh for logical discrepancies), and guessed each elector's religion from their name and their relative's name. On that guess, Muslims were 13.6% of the draft roll, 7.6% of the unmapped and 20.3% of those flagged for logical discrepancies, and 30% of those flagged for the five reasons that turn on family size, such as six or more electors naming the same parent. The paper reports that ERONET, the Commission's software, decided who was flagged, that no SIR order mentioned notices for discrepancies before the Commission's direction of 14 May 2026, which still did not set out the reasons, and that the Commission had not answered its questions.

items.title: An entitled generation and an Opposition that protests too much
items.shows: It argues that the gap between the final rolls and the adult population mostly reflects adults who do not register, which he puts at 8.5 per cent of adults from the young missing from the 2024 roll. On that benchmark he estimates about 70 lakh eligible people kept off the rolls of Bihar and eight phase II states, and about 50 lakh in West Bengal alone. He criticises the haste of the revision and the new Form 6 declaration, and asks the Commission to publish deletions by reason, state and booth.

items.title: Much Ado About (Almost) Nothing
items.shows: It is the longer version of his column. It sets out his estimate of adults, his benchmark of 8.5 per cent of adults not registering, a clean roll for each of nine states with final rolls, and sections on Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Assam. He puts the eligible people kept off the rolls at about 70 lakh, with a range of 10 lakh to 1.3 crore, and states which of his figures are his own calculations.

items.title: Let’s not be in denial — disenfranchisement in real
items.shows: It is a reply to Surjit Bhalla that sets the final rolls of nine states against the Technical Group's projected adults for 2026 and finds the rolls about 7 crore, or almost 12 per cent, short, with Uttar Pradesh 2.8 crore short. The authors extend the rate to about 12 crore missing voters nationally, and to about 14 crore on another analyst's estimate of the final rolls, and they say the gap includes adults who were never enrolled. They dispute Bhalla's allowance for young adults who do not register. The print edition carries a table by state.

items.title: Long & short of SIR: What happens when exclusion is prioritised over inclusion
items.shows: This is Drèze's follow-up to the column he wrote with Yogendra Yadav in The Indian Express. He sets the rolls of the major states against the Technical Group's projected adults for 2026 and finds them at 99 per cent before the revision and 85 per cent in the draft lists, and the twelve states with final lists at 97, 86 and 88 per cent. He argues that the rolls before the revision already missed many adults, perhaps up to 10 per cent on what he calls patchy evidence, and that dead, shifted and duplicate names hid the gap. Ground reports suggest most deletions of absent, shifted, dead and duplicate electors were legitimate, he writes. In his account the gap stayed because the second stage demanded documents from electors who were unmapped or had logical discrepancies, when large-scale use of Form 6 could have enrolled the adults who were missing. Assam and Himachal Pradesh are left out of his table.

items.title: Election Commission Seeks to Remove Half the Bengal Voters Judges Have Cleared For Inclusion
items.shows: From appeal records collected by the Civic Research Group, it counts the Election Commission's appeals before West Bengal's SIR tribunals against voters whom judicial officers had found eligible, 14,75,887 of 30,00,545 by 17 October, set out by district and seat, by the minority share of each seat and by the 2026 result, with how few appeals the tribunals had decided.

items.title: SIR: Over 76,000 applications seeking inclusion rejected; net additions far lower than draft stage deletions
items.shows: The Chief Electoral Officer's office gave Karnataka's figures for applications received from 16 June to 23 September. Of 7,87,534 Form 6 applications, 7,08,110 were accepted and 76,176 rejected, against more than 80.62 lakh names left off the draft roll as shifted or absent. Of 58,475 Form 7 applications, 23,926 were accepted. The office had not yet released counts of voters found ineligible.

items.title: Surjit Bhalla: SIR needs reform. But let’s go by numbers, not protestors’ slogans
items.shows: It replies to Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav. For the nine states with final rolls, it takes the figures of 59.9 crore adults and 52.8 crore names, allows for 5.2 crore young people who were not registered in 2024 and 1.5% of adults for older people who never registered, and puts the eligible people wrongly left off at about 1 crore. It also lists what the Commission has not published, including a national roll after the revision and deletions by reason, state and booth.

items.title: Karnataka’s most backward districts see low applications for inclusion after SIR draft deletions
items.shows: The paper sets district figures from Karnataka's Chief Electoral Officer for Kalaburagi, Mysuru, Raichur and Ballari, where more than 18% of the electorate was left off the draft roll, against the Form 6 applications received by 23 September. Mysuru received 35,447 against more than 5.57 lakh left off. The office has not released the age of applicants, so first-time voters cannot be told apart from those seeking to return.

items.title: 90% of 33 lakh SIR cases ‘resolved’ or ‘parked for final roll’ in Delhi
items.shows: The Delhi Chief Electoral Officer's office said on 23 October that about 29.5 lakh of the nearly 33 lakh notice cases, 13.79 lakh unmapped and 19.33 lakh flagged for logical discrepancies, had been resolved or parked for the final roll. It did not say how many were rejected. The report also gives the Form 6 count since the draft roll, 2,50,754, and Maharashtra's proposal to change Form 6 for voters seeking to return.

items.title: Irregularities in Voter Lists Like Pilibhit Could Alter UP's Electoral Outcome. Here's Why
items.shows: It sets the Samajwadi Party's list of 100 constituencies where the party alleges duplicate entries against the 2022 Assembly results, and finds that 43 of them were seats the party narrowly won or lost. It counts 124 seats won by fewer than 10,000 votes in 2022 and 53 by fewer than 5,000, beside the 10,470 entries the Chief Electoral Officer's inquiry found in Pilibhit, a seat the BJP won by 6,970 votes.

items.title: Revisiting India’s first general election, 1951–52
items.shows: The Hindu's visual story retells India's first general election, which began in Chini and Pangi in Himachal Pradesh on 25 October 1951 and ran until February 1952. By the paper's account, provincial and State governments were asked in November 1947 to plan the preparation of electoral rolls, compiling began in November 1950, Bihar, Orissa and Punjab were among the last to publish preliminary rolls in March 1951, and the final rolls were published in November 1951. It puts those eligible to vote at around 17.3 crore and those who voted at 10.6 crore, and says around 28 lakh entries for women listed only as someone's wife or mother were deleted because the Commission insisted that women be registered in their own names. It also covers Sukumar Sen, the first Chief Election Commissioner, Shyam Saran Negi, remembered as the first voter, the separate ballot box for each candidate, the results and some of the close contests.

items.title: The SIR and its error margin
items.shows: Nishtha Gupta, a technology policy researcher based in New Delhi, argues that the revision replaced the presumption the Supreme Court set out in 1995, that a name already on the roll is there lawfully, with data matching by software. She describes rolls from the last intensive revision, mostly of 2002, digitised and transliterated into English by machine and then matched against the new enumeration forms, followed by tests for logical discrepancies such as a parent and child less than 15 years apart. By her account those who failed these tests included twins, Oraon voters whose surname Xalxo was rendered as Khalkho, and voters whose father's name was Md. in one list and Mohammed in the other, and according to the Internet Freedom Foundation the rules flagged 17% of West Bengal's electors and 41% of Madhya Pradesh's. She cites 91% of decided exclusion appeals in West Bengal going in the appellant's favour, 728 of 729 voters cut at one booth in Delhi's Bela Estate, and about 200 notices for each booth level officer in Delhi to verify within a very tight deadline. She asks the Commission to publish its matching rules and error rates, to open itself to an independent audit, and to delete no name until an officer with the time and authority has verified the person behind the record.

items.title: Before UP polls, let’s ask: Does voter list meet criteria of completeness, equity, accuracy
items.shows: Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav put Uttar Pradesh's adult population at an estimated 16.2 crore on 1 March 2026 against 13.4 crore names on the final roll of April 2026, down from 15.4 crore before the revision, and conclude that about 2.8 crore voters, or 17.3% of adults, appear to be missing. They reply to Surjit Bhalla's estimate of a shortfall of 20 lakh, which treats all non-enrolment as voluntary and builds on the nearly 40% of the state's adults aged 18 to 29 who were not enrolled in 2024, and say that with the figure for 2019 his shortfall would be 93 lakh. As further evidence they cite the State Election Commission's parallel revision of the rural roll, which ended at 12.6 crore and, with the unrevised urban list of 2023, gives 16.9 crore voters in the state. They hold that the final roll seems to fail on completeness, equity and accuracy, and that the shortfall works against women and young voters.

items.title: SIR: Karnataka 64.5 lakh voters ‘short’; foreign nationals still ‘uncounted’
items.shows: The News Minute sets the final roll of 4,54,55,689 general electors against about 5.19 crore people old enough to vote in a projected Karnataka population of about 6.89 crore on 1 March 2026, and finds the roll about 64.5 lakh short. It cites the Chief Electoral Officer's elector to population ratio of 66.11. By its calculation 38.41 lakh of the shortfall, or 59.5%, are aged 18 to 29. It reports the Chief Electoral Officer, V. Anbu Kumar, saying that out of more than 43.82 lakh notices for logical discrepancies and unmapped entries at least 1,88,324 names were deleted from the final roll, with 61,867 marked ineligible, and that the foreign nationals found number less than a thousand and are still being identified. It cites the Times of India for a figure of 716 foreign nationals, and reports that the Commission has ordered special drives and a fresh look at constituencies, wards and booths where deletions were high.

items.title: SIR: Of over a crore deletion, 4.48 lakh return; one-third additions are first-time voters
items.shows: From the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer's figures, The Hindu finds that 2,59,838 of the 7,08,110 Form 6 applications accepted, out of 7,87,534 received between 16 June and 23 September, came from electors aged 18 and 19, about 36%. It reads the remaining 4.48 lakh as the people left off the draft who got back on the roll, against about 1.07 crore left off. All the accepted applications together come to about seven for every 100 names left off. It puts more than 84.46 lakh of those left off in the absent and shifted categories, with 7.09 lakh duplicates and 16.39 lakh dead. Bengaluru fell from 1.03 crore electors before the revision to 59.08 lakh in the final roll, with a net 2.74 lakh added during claims, of whom 41,141 were aged 18 and 19. Kalaburagi lost more than 5.21 lakh names at the draft and gained a net 44,559 by the final roll. The paper takes every accepted Form 6 from an elector older than 19 to be a name left off the draft, which the data it gives does not show.

items.title: Karnataka SIR 2026: Preliminary Report on Electoral Roll Deletions
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Ashin Chakraborty, Souptik Halder
items.shows: From the lists of names left off Karnataka's draft roll of 24 August 2026 for all 224 constituencies, the Sabar Institute counts 1,08,24,651 names with a recorded reason, which it puts at 20.4% of the 2023 roll. It finds 15.1% marked dead, and it describes the other 91,85,436, marked shifted, untraceable or absent, already enrolled elsewhere or as having refused the form, as alive. It reports that Bengaluru Urban has 18% of the state's electors and 44% of the names, and that in Bommanahalli, C.V. Raman Nagar, Dasarahalli, B.T.M. Layout and Vijay Nagar more names were left off than votes were cast in 2023. It finds 2,102 of the 4,926 third gender electors on the 2023 roll, 42.7%, on the lists. Among electors aged 18 to 29 marked a reason other than death it counts about three women for every two men, and nearly two for one outside Bengaluru. Outside Bengaluru Urban, by its correlations, districts with more Scheduled Caste residents and districts with lower income per head had more names left off.

items.title: Post-SIR, voter base in 5 poll-bound states shrank by up to 13.24 per cent
items.shows: PTI sets out the rolls of the five states due to vote early next year, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Manipur and Goa, before the revision, at the draft and at the final roll, from figures the Election Commission and the Chief Electoral Officers published. By its count the five rolls fell from about 18.71 crore to 16.43 crore, a fall of about 2.29 crore or 12.2 per cent, and Uttar Pradesh accounts for nearly 90 per cent of it. It gives the fall in the roll as 13.24 per cent in Uttar Pradesh, 10.76 per cent in Goa, 10.07 per cent in Uttarakhand, 6.34 per cent in Punjab and 6.33 per cent in Manipur. For Uttar Pradesh it gives 15.44 crore electors before the revision, 12.56 crore on the draft and 13.40 crore on the final roll, with about 2.89 crore names left off the draft. PTI says about 0.84 crore of those, roughly 29 per cent, were restored, and it describes about 34 per cent in Punjab, about 17 per cent in Manipur and about 3 per cent in Uttarakhand as names that came back. Each of those figures measures the rise from the draft to the final roll, which is the names added after the draft, new voters among them, less the names deleted after it. The report does not say how many of the names added had been left off the draft. Goa's final roll is smaller than its draft.

items.title: SIR Maharashtra: Preliminary Report (2026)
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Ashin Chakraborty, Souptik Halder
items.shows: From the lists of names left off Maharashtra's draft roll for all 288 constituencies, the Sabar Institute counts 2,06,88,421 names, 21.1% of the 9,78,54,049 electors on the roll before the revision, and finds 16.8% of them marked dead. It describes the other 1,72,06,190, marked permanently shifted, untraceable or absent, or already enrolled elsewhere, as alive. It reports that Mumbai's 36 constituencies have 11% of the state's electors and 17% of the names, that in Colaba more names were left off than votes were cast in 2024, and that names left off for a reason other than death exceed the 2024 winning margin in 190 of the 288 seats. It finds 3,250 of the 6,101 third gender electors on the 2024 roll, 53.3%, on the lists. Outside Mumbai, among electors aged 18 to 29 marked permanently shifted, it counts 8,22,798 women and 3,79,991 men, which it reads as consistent with women moving to a husband's home after marriage. The roll has no column for religion, and Sabar classifies the names by religion itself, from the elector's name and the name of the parent or spouse, as a statistical estimate for aggregate figures. By that classification names it counts as Muslim are 14.6% of the names left off, against about 12.1% expected from the 2011 Census. By the same classification, comparing names of the same age in the same seat, the odds of a name it counts as Muslim being marked already enrolled elsewhere, against being marked dead, are 2.07 times those of other names. The report says that name-based matching for duplicates is one possible cause, which the lists do not let it test, and that none of this proves any group was targeted. It finds no difference between the seats of the two alliances once Mumbai, region, reservation, urbanisation and size are allowed for, and the strongest link is with low turnout in 2024. The office of Maharashtra's Chief Electoral Officer replied on 7 November that electors marked dead or already enrolled are a little over 25% of the names and those marked absent or shifted about 75%, that comparing Mumbai and Thane with the state average is not appropriate, and that the revision is still under way, PTI reported.

items.title: Muslim electorate in Karnataka shrinks 18.84 per cent after SIR, slightly above State average
items.shows: Frontline reports estimates by Sankalp, a political research consultancy in Karnataka, of how the fall in Karnataka's roll divides by religion. The roll does not record religion, and the magazine says Sankalp's figures by religion are estimates. Karnataka's roll fell from 5.54 crore electors before the revision to 4.55 crore on the final roll, or 17.9 per cent. By Sankalp's estimate Muslim electors fell from 71.56 lakh to 58.08 lakh, or 18.84 per cent, and other electors from 4.82 crore to 3.96 crore, or 17.79 per cent, so the Muslim share of the roll went from 12.91 per cent to 12.77 per cent. In Bengaluru's 28 seats the roll fell from 1.03 crore to 59.08 lakh, and Sankalp puts the fall at 33.72 per cent for Muslim electors and 43.82 per cent for others. In the other 196 seats it puts the fall at 15.32 per cent for Muslim electors and 12.18 per cent for others. The political analyst Sandeep Shastri tells the magazine that Bengaluru's roll had long been inflated by electors living abroad or voting in their home towns. Of the 1,07,96,339 names left off the draft, Sankalp estimates that 15.43 lakh were of Muslim electors and 92.32 lakh of others. It also counts 39 of the 224 seats where booths that gave 60 per cent or more of their votes in the 2024 Lok Sabha election to the Congress hold more than 35 per cent of the seat's names left off the draft. Across those 39 seats 42 per cent of the names left off are in such booths, and 26 of the seats are held by the Congress, 11 by the BJP and 2 by the Janata Dal (Secular). Frontline reports, from sources in the office of Karnataka's Chief Electoral Officer, that 716 foreign nationals were found on the roll, 641 of them from Nepal.

items.title: Is the SIR Led by a Remote-Controlled Computer?
items.shows: Rajeev Kumar, a former professor of computer science at IIT Kharagpur, IIT Kanpur, BITS Pilani and JNU, argues that a roll of nearly a billion electors needs a computerised database and that the trouble with the revision lies in poor governance of the exercise. He sets out six weaknesses as he sees them. The rolls of 2002 to 2004, prepared largely on paper and digitised later, are used to map electors without being checked first. The rules for logical discrepancies are not public and reportedly grew from six categories to eleven. Reports allege bulk deletions with no identifiable applicant and inserted code that generated Form 7 objections, which he says need an independent inquiry. Reports of restricted access suggest registration officers could not verify, correct or restore records. He says a pilot should have tested the mapping, the rules and the forms before the exercise began, and the Commission declined in reply to an RTI request to describe the software that flags errors. He asks for a separate form or workflow to restore wrongly deleted names in place of Form 6, and for an independent technical audit of ECINet by industry experts, possibly led by Nandan Nilekani, and he says the academic review proposed in the Commission's press note of 26 September may not be enough.

items.title: 27.59% Voters Deleted From Ten Karnataka Assembly Constituencies Represented by Muslim MLAs
items.shows: The Wire carries Vartha Bharati's analysis of figures from Sankalp, a political research consultancy, drawn from the booth-wise lists of names left off Karnataka's draft that the Chief Electoral Officer published. It calls a booth Congress strong where the Congress won 60 per cent or more of the votes in the 2024 Lok Sabha election. Of the 1,07,76,645 names left off that the analysis could place, it finds 22,35,155, or 20.74 per cent, in such booths. In 39 of the 224 seats more than 35 per cent of the names left off are in such booths, and those 39 seats hold 19,85,732 names left off, or 18.4 per cent of the total. The Congress won 26 of the 39 in 2023, the BJP 11 and the Janata Dal (Secular) 2. By Sankalp's estimate Muslims are on average 22 per cent of the roll in the 39 seats, against 12.9 per cent across the state. The roll does not record religion, so a share by religion is an estimate. The article also sets the 10,08,038 additions the Commission recorded against the 7,85,716 applications for inclusion that Sankalp tracked in the Form 9 lists from 16 June 2026, a difference of 2,22,322, and says the Commission has published no reconciliation of the two. It repeats the figures for the ten seats held by Muslim MLAs and for Muslim electors left off as absent and as already enrolled, which the Karnataka Rajya Muslim Okkoota released on 9 November.

items.title: No eligible citizen is left out (?)
items.shows: Aman Bhargava of Diagram Chasing tests the line printed on every page of the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer's summary booklet for the final roll, that no eligible citizen is left out and no ineligible person is included, against the rolls themselves. He read all 60,923 booth files of the final roll of 27 October by machine and joined them by EPIC number to digitised copies of the 2002 roll, the January 2025 roll, the list of names left off the draft and the notice lists, which the groups Mathakaavalu and Edellu Karnataka made. He reports that of 1,05,48,148 electors left off the draft whom he found on the January 2025 roll, about 14,900 came back on the final roll in the same constituency with the same name, relative and age, and that 206 of 8.9 lakh aged 75 and over came back. He counts 3,115 electors told they were not on the 2002 roll although the Chief Electoral Officer's own copy of it carries them under the same EPIC number, 4,954 deleted after a notice that flagged children born less than nine months apart, a rule that catches twins, 8,992 people on the roll more than once in their own booth, 461 EPIC numbers on the roll in two constituencies and 234 new voters in Dasarahalli given an EPIC number held earlier by someone left off the draft. He finds the share of electors sent a notice ranging from 0.03 per cent in Mayakonda to 59 per cent in C.V. Raman Nagar, and nine constituencies where no notice ended in a finding of ineligibility. He says his counts are minimums, that the rolls by themselves cannot establish identity, and that the work rests on optical character recognition of files the Commission publishes as PDFs.

items.title: The SIR exercise is also a technology failure
items.shows: Priya Seetharaman, a professor in the Management Information Systems Group at the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta, reads the revision as a digital project run through the Commission's ERONet platform, and finds it fails tests that a large system rollout is expected to pass. She writes that notices for logical discrepancy were raised centrally by filters such as the gap in age between parent and child and the number of children linked to one parent, although ages on Indian rolls are often approximate, and that a rule coded into the platform, never published by the Commission, decides who must appear for a hearing. She says matching an elector to a parent on the 2002 roll compares family names across decades and scripts without having been tested at scale, citing West Bengal's 2002 rolls, which were in Bengali and were rendered into English, reportedly with machine tools, over 1.3 crore entries flagged there, and counsel's statement to the Supreme Court that more than half the logical discrepancy cases were variations in names. She writes that features changed while the revision was under way, among them de-duplication software the Commission had told the Supreme Court in late 2025 could not be relied on and later switched back on in some States and Union Territories, and a mapping check that made booth level officers redo finished work. She says new ERONet options in October letting registration officers dispose of notice cases without hearings were explained through demonstration videos, and that such instructions often came through video conferences and WhatsApp groups after the software had already been changed to enforce them, so that the software stood in for the written rule. She adds that the online Form 6 carried a declaration on parents and grandparents that is not in the statutory form. On the timetable, she notes that enumeration in Tamil Nadu and West Bengal ran about six weeks with final rolls in February for polls in April, and that West Bengal's final roll was published with over half a crore names still under adjudication.
