items.title: Rajasthan Counted Voters Thrice In Under a Year. The Numbers Changed Every Time.
items.shows: The Wire sets side by side the three counts of Rajasthan's electors made in 2026. The final roll of the Special Intensive Revision held 5.15 crore electors, the draft roll of the special summary revision now under way holds 5.26 crore, and the State Election Commission's final roll for the panchayat and municipal elections holds 5.45 crore. It explains that the Election Commission prepares the rolls for Lok Sabha and Assembly elections under Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act, 1950, while State Election Commissions prepare the rolls for panchayat and municipal elections under Articles 243K and 243ZA. It reports, from the Times of India, that the State Election Commission's secretary Rajesh Verma said his office built its rolls from the Commission's roll from before the revision, as last updated on 1 January 2025, because preparations for the local elections began before the revision was over. It cites a comparison by Nikhil Dey, a founder of the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, which found 26.63 lakh electors deleted in the revision still on the State Election Commission's local body rolls, and his question how people the revision found dead could be on the state's roll. It notes that the claims and objections of the summary revision may change the count again by January 2027.

items.title: 26L deleted in Rajasthan post-SIR still on panchayat poll rolls: PUCL
items.shows: The Times of India reports an analysis by the People's Union for Civil Liberties, dated 11 November, which found that more than 26 lakh of the 41.65 lakh electors deleted from Rajasthan's draft roll in the Special Intensive Revision are still on the State Election Commission's rolls for the 2026 panchayat and urban local body elections, 13.7 lakh on the panchayat rolls and 12.4 lakh on the municipal rolls. The analysis covers the State Election Commission's second supplement to the panchayat rolls, published up to 12 October. By PUCL's count these include 3,20,395 people the Election Commission marked dead, more than 17.32 lakh it deleted as shifted, 3.67 lakh as untraceable or absent and more than 1.83 lakh as enrolled elsewhere. Baran has the highest share of deleted electors still on the State Election Commission's rolls, 83.1%, followed by Pali, Jalore, Bikaner, Sirohi and Deedwana-Kuchaman, all above 80%. Of those marked dead, 70.7% in Banswara are still on the rolls, and PUCL says that in seven districts at least half of those marked dead are still on them. The figure is 69,343 lower than PUCL's earlier count of nearly 26.7 lakh from the panchayat rolls of 25 February, and the number marked dead and still listed fell by 31,987 from 3,52,382. PUCL puts the active names across the State Election Commission's rolls at 5,47,86,896, which is 32,72,934 or 6.4% more than the Election Commission's final roll of 5,15,13,962. The State Election Commission's secretary Rajesh Verma told the paper that the state's roll numbers have increased in recent months and that the update process likely reduced the gap.

items.title: Special Summary Revision: About 50 lakh voters added across 9 states; fraction of SIR removals
items.shows: Hindustan Times sets the draft rolls of the special summary revision, published on 12 November, against the final rolls of the intensive revision and reports about 50 lakh electors added across the nine states and union territories for which figures were released, with rises of 0.1% to 3%. It gives Bihar about 7.55 crore electors, about 13 lakh more than its final roll of 7.42 crore. It gives Tamil Nadu about 5.77 crore, about 10 lakh more than its final roll and below the 6.41 crore it held before the intensive revision. It gives Madhya Pradesh 8.19 lakh more for nearly 5.48 crore, Rajasthan a rise of 2.22% or about 11 lakh, and Kerala 2.736 crore against 2.695 crore, about 4.06 lakh more. It puts the largest rise in Goa, about 3%, with about 43,000 names added and at least 11,000 deleted. It gives Uttarakhand 1,25,216 names added and 6,130 applications for deletion processed, and Manipur about 33,700 more. It sets the additions beside the fall in the rolls from about 50.9 crore to 44.4 crore at the drafts of the intensive revision's second phase in 12 states and union territories, and it says applicants in the summary revision do not have to submit documents proving citizenship or be mapped to earlier rolls. It reports that Uttar Pradesh moved its draft to 17 November, that claims and objections close on 11 December and that the final rolls are due on 4 January.

items.title: SIR vs SSR: Voter rolls in 13 states and UTs add 74.66 lakh names, register 1.65% rise
items.shows: Deccan Herald sets the draft rolls of the special summary revision in 13 states and union territories against the final rolls of the intensive revision, and of Assam's special revision, and reports that their rolls grew from 45.22 crore to 45.96 crore. It says these states and union territories held 49.61 crore electors before the intensive revision. It gives the largest rise in numbers to Uttar Pradesh, 18.84 lakh or 1.4%, from 13.39 crore to 13.58 crore, and puts Bihar next, with its roll rising from 7.42 crore to 7.55 crore. It gives Rajasthan 11.47 lakh or 2.23%, Tamil Nadu 10.39 lakh or 1.83%, Kerala 4.06 lakh or 1.51%, Chhattisgarh 2.85 lakh or 1.53%, Assam 2.18 lakh or 0.88%, Uttarakhand 1.19 lakh or 1.66%, Manipur 33,737 or 1.72%, Puducherry 12,786 or 1.35% and Lakshadweep 94 or 0.16%. It puts the largest rise in proportion in Goa, 3.01%, from 10.57 lakh to 10.89 lakh. It reports that drafts had been published in 15 states, with no data for Punjab and Gujarat, and that the summary revision was announced in Karnataka and Meghalaya on 16 November. It reports that the Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised concerns over the delay in holding the summary revision in states where the intensive revision had finished. It reports that parties will now be given the draft and final rolls free of cost as readable PDFs without photographs of the electors, along with a physical copy, and that the Commission had earlier refused machine-readable rolls.

items.title: SIR Uttar Pradesh: Preliminary Report 2026
items.authors: Sabir Ahamed, Ashin Chakraborty, Souptik Halder
items.shows: From the lists of names left off Uttar Pradesh's draft roll of 6 January 2026 for all 403 constituencies, the Sabar Institute counts 2,88,71,423 names, which it puts at 18.7% of the 15,44,30,092 electors on the roll before the revision, and finds 16.0% of them marked dead. It describes the other 2,42,48,090, marked permanently shifted, untraceable or absent, or already enrolled elsewhere, as alive, and says half of them are under 40. By its count 22.0% of the women and 16.5% of the men on the 2022 roll are among the names left off. The report measures these two shares against the 2022 roll because it is the latest roll split by sex, so they are shares of a different roll from the 18.7%. Outside the four city districts, among electors aged 18 to 29 marked permanently shifted, it counts 19,18,015 women and 5,37,217 men, which it reads as consistent with women moving to a husband's home after marriage. It reports that Lucknow, Ghaziabad, Gautam Buddha Nagar and Kanpur Nagar have 7.8% of the state's electors and 11.7% of the names, that Lucknow's names left off are 30.0% of its roll before the revision, and that in Allahabad North more names were left off than votes were cast in 2022. It finds that names left off for a reason other than death exceed the 2022 winning margin in 359 of the 403 seats, and names marked untraceable or absent alone in 194. It finds 1,805 of the 8,855 third gender electors on the 2022 roll, 20.4%, on the lists, and finds low turnout in 2022 the measure most closely linked to more names left off for a reason other than death. The report says the roll does not record religion, and that it estimates religion from the elector's and the relative's names with the Institute's own model. The report analyses the lists of names left off the draft roll, and Uttar Pradesh's final roll was published on 10 April 2026 with 13,39,84,792 electors. The report says that some of the people on the lists will have applied again and may appear on the final roll, and that correlation is not causation.

items.title: Transgender Voters Are Disappearing From Electoral Rolls at More Than Twice the Overall Rate
items.shows: Vaivab Das, a doctoral scholar at IIT Delhi, writes in The Wire on the Transgender Day of Remembrance that electors registered as transgender fell much faster than the electorate in 12 states and union territories. By the article's own tabulation of the Election Commission's statistical records and the summaries the Chief Electoral Officers released, electors in Assam, Bihar, Delhi, Goa, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Odisha, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal fell from 62.6 crore to 55.1 crore, or 11.91%, while transgender electors fell from 35,870 to 24,811, or 30.8%. It gives the largest falls as Delhi (65%), Maharashtra (49%), Karnataka (43%) and Uttar Pradesh (37%). The article's set includes Assam, which had a Special Revision in place of the intensive one, and where its table shows the whole roll growing. The article labels its earlier figures 2024 or 2025. Its later totals for Delhi, Maharashtra and Karnataka equal their draft rolls and its later total for Odisha equals Odisha's final roll, so its falls set drafts beside final rolls. It also sets the 2024 Lok Sabha rolls against the 2011 Census count of transgender persons. It quotes a trans masculine person working in Bengaluru, under a changed name, who says that after he applied using his parents' entry in the 2002 roll a notice told him his name and his father's name did not match, and that the booth level officer then asked for his father's documents although he has not been in touch with his family for ten years. The author argues that tying enrolment to the family puts at risk the vote of transgender people who have left their families.

items.title: ECI’s software use needs reconsideration
items.shows: Joseph C. Mathew, a former IT adviser to the Government of Keralam, argues that the Commission's use of software needs to be reconsidered. He writes that under section 13B of the Representation of the People Act the sole authority for editing the voters' list is entrusted to local Electoral Registration Officers and Booth Level Officers, and that the Commission's centralised ECINet and ERONet software has effectively stripped them of their legally mandated powers. In his view the Commission appears in the process to have created its own Act and Rules. He recalls that in 2015 the Commission linked voter IDs with Aadhaar data under the National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme, which he describes as a mass elimination of voters using centralised software, until the Supreme Court put an end to it. Most of the piece concerns electronic voting machines, where he argues from two Supreme Court judgments that the safeguards the Commission has presented do not make the system foolproof. He closes by saying that a reconsideration is necessary at a time when the Commission is using software “to dictate addition in the electoral list itself”.

items.title: Uttar Pradesh voter rolls, 2024 to 2027
items.shows: s1d labs has read four of Uttar Pradesh's electoral rolls from the Election Commission's PDFs into tables, one file for each of the 403 assembly constituencies: the roll of the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the draft and final rolls of the Special Intensive Revision and the draft roll of the 2027 summary revision. It says it read about 6.8 lakh PDFs, most of them scanned images, with five optical character readers and no language model, and that the 2027 roll, the only one of the four with a text layer, was read directly. By its own count, leaving out entries with a deleted mark, the 2024 roll holds 15,36,26,796 entries, the SIR draft 12,28,31,737, the SIR final 13,11,70,043 and the 2027 draft 13,58,67,928. Its README says that about 4,015 newer parts of the two SIR rolls are missing from its files, which it estimates at about 2.5 million voters in each roll, and it asks readers not to compare its SIR totals with the Commission's state totals until that gap is closed. It reports that a hand check of 402 boxes found every field right in 96.77 per cent of SIR records. In the files it publishes, names, relatives' names, EPIC numbers and house numbers are replaced by keyed-hash tokens, so that one elector can be followed from roll to roll and counted by age and gender, and it says the tokens do not make a record anonymous. It sends the full text to journalists and researchers who apply. It says the Commission's PDFs remain the authority and its counts are not official figures.

items.title: SIR and the BJP's Bengal Majority
items.shows: It is an economist's counterfactual. Even if every elector deleted after adjudication had voted for the runner-up, the BJP keeps a majority, and only under assumptions the data do not support do the wider counts of names left off or deleted overturn it.

items.title: Power Without Oversight: India’s SIR Judgment and the Unfinished Business of Institutional Design
items.shows: It reads the Supreme Court's SIR judgment against the scholarship on independent electoral bodies and argues that the Commission holds wide power over the rolls without matching accountability.

items.title: How the Invisible Maths of Electoral Roll Revision Altered West Bengal's Election
items.shows: It is an arithmetic test of sensitivity. The gross count of names left off or deleted exceeded the winning margin in 160 seats, and of two no-SIR scenarios one returns the TMC and the other leaves the BJP with a smaller majority. It does not model voter preference.

items.title: Analysis and Explainer on the Software of the SIR That Runs Without Transparency
items.shows: It describes the systems behind the revision (ECINET, the BLO app, ERONET run by TCS since 2023, the mapping and 'logical discrepancy' rules, machine transliteration and duplicate-detection tools) and finds that none has a published specification, threshold or audit. Citing The Reporters' Collective, it gives 1.31 crore electors flagged in West Bengal and 2.35 crore in Madhya Pradesh by the discrepancy rules.

items.title: India: Mass Voter Roll Exclusions Deeply Flawed
items.shows: Human Rights Watch says it has interviewed 70 people in Delhi, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Karnataka since August, among them 40 whose families were affected by the revision, former election commissioners, lawyers, activists and a serving electoral official. It finds that people were excluded for mismatched names, spelling errors, having six or more siblings or siblings born less than nine months apart, and that the software flagged Adivasi and Muslim names disproportionately, in part because their spellings vary. It finds that the authorities used data from the revision to deny passport renewals, food rations, a West Bengal cash transfer for women, scholarships and residence certificates, including to people whose appeals were still pending. It describes the bulk use of Form 7 against Muslim voters as the media reported it, transgender people excluded because their documents carry different names, and security forces beating and arresting protesters in October 2026. Its Asia director, Elaine Pearson, calls for the revision to be scrapped and for everyone wrongly excluded to regain the vote promptly.

items.title: SIR applies a decade of exclusion lessons perfected on welfare schemes
items.shows: Veena Naregal, Professor of Sociology at the Institute of Economic Growth, Delhi, argues that the SIR carries over to the vote a method the Commission first tried on voter rolls in 2015 and that was refined on welfare lists in the decade since, which she calls freeze-and-prune, where a past list is the test of present entitlement and correction is slow. She traces the 2015 drive to link voter cards with Aadhaar, the order of 20 March 2015 that froze each state's ration numbers at 2011 levels and told states to check ration lists against voter lists, and the health insurance scheme's fixed pool of 10.74 crore families from the 2011 Socio-Economic and Caste Census. She sets the 2003 revision, which used the existing roll as its base, against the SIR's reliance on a roll two decades old, and notes that the Commission certified a national roll of 96.88 crore electors in February 2024. She names four kinds of exclusion the SIR creates and points to unpublished software rules that flag logical discrepancies and unmapped electors for notice and deletion.

items.title: Voters and Citizens: From Inclusion to Exclusion in Contemporary India
items.shows: Niraja Gopal Jayal, who holds the Avantha Chair at King's College London, argues in an essay first published in Indian Politics and Policy in spring 2026, and republished with a postscript written in November 2026, that the revision of the rolls shares the exclusionary tendencies that she traces in India's citizenship law since 1985. She sets the inclusive making of the first roll from 1947 against the Assam National Register of Citizens and the amendments of 1985, 2003 and 2019, and reads the Supreme Court's judgment of 27 May 2026 as endorsing the Commission's power to examine citizenship before it enrols a voter. In her account the revision moved the work of verification from the booth level officer's visits to the voter, who is deleted for failing to submit the enumeration form, and the Commission's change to Form 7 in 2022 let anyone from the same assembly constituency object to a name. She gives West Bengal's figures as about 6.4 million routine deletions, 2.7 million names under adjudication and 0.188 million added, and counts 7.4 million deleted in Tamil Nadu and 6.81 million in Gujarat. She writes that the burden falls disproportionately on Dalits, Muslims and women, and that the abuse of Form 7 by Booth Level Agents of the BJP to target Muslim voters has been reported from several states. In the postscript she puts Karnataka's deletions at one crore, about 18% of the electorate, says the roll is being used to deny welfare benefits although the Supreme Court ruled the revision cannot be used for other purposes, and says that only scrapping the revision and returning to the earlier rolls can put this right.

items.title: US religious freedom panel says India is targeting minorities in voter roll revisions
items.shows: Reuters reports a statement of 19 November by the US Commission on International Religious Freedom, which it describes as a bipartisan body of the US government that monitors religious freedom around the world and makes recommendations that are not binding. It quotes the commission's chair, Asif Mahmood, as saying that the Indian government is targeting Muslim citizens by removing them from voter rolls, calling them foreigners and now illegally deporting them. It quotes a commissioner, Gene Mills, calling the government's expulsion of its own citizens on the basis of their faith a shocking escalation, and reports that he urged the State Department to designate India a country of particular concern. Reuters reports that Washington has not acted on the commission's recent recommendations on India, that India's foreign ministry has called the commission biased, and that the Indian embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. It reports that the Election Commission says it was removing duplicate, dead, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters and that anyone excluded in error can appeal, and that the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last month that the issue was a domestic political matter on which Washington would not comment.

items.title: “So What’s This Democracy We’re Talking About?”: Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India
items.shows: Human Rights Watch says in a 95-page report on India's institutions that the Election Commission faces what it calls a massive crisis of credibility. It says the revision begun in June 2025 had deleted over 130 million names by October 2026, in a process it describes as arbitrary and opaque, and that it disproportionately excluded women, people living in poverty, religious minorities, particularly Muslims, and other marginalised communities. It describes the rules as changing across three phases. In Bihar voters had to give one of 11 documents, in the second phase they had to trace themselves or a parent to the rolls of the 2002 to 2006 revisions and names were deleted for what the Commission called logical discrepancies, and in the third phase Form 6 was changed to ask whether an applicant's parents or grandparents were in the last revision, a change it says two election commissioners reportedly objected to. It says the Commission directed that electors deleted from the roll be enrolled again on Form 6, which in its account required them to declare falsely that they were applying for the first time. It says about 93 percent of the West Bengal electors whose appeals were decided were restored, that the Calcutta High Court said the over 3.4 million appeals still pending would take at least 21 years to resolve, and that information on deleted electors was used to halt passport renewals and to deny access to social security programmes and residence certificates for students. It finds that the Commission has failed to hold the Prime Minister and senior BJP leaders to account for apparent violations of the code of conduct and to investigate allegations of irregularities credibly, and that the law of December 2023 entrenched the executive's control over the appointment of election commissioners. It recommends that the revision be scrapped at once and that an independent investigation be set up into allegations of politically motivated interference. The report rests on more than 40 interviews held between January 2025 and September 2026 and on published sources.

items.title: Supreme Court Upholds Election Commission's Power To Conduct SIR Of Electoral Rolls, Says It Advances Free & Fair Elections
items.shows: It reports the Supreme Court judgment in ADR v. Election Commission holding the SIR within the Commission's powers and its procedure lawful, with a nexus to free and fair elections.

items.title: Bihar SIR Judgement: Three doctrinal gaps
items.shows: It argues that the judgment of 27 May 2026 relies on one half of the 2024 Section 6A ruling, accepts the Commission's reasons for a special revision without a record behind them, and treats the 1995 Lal Babu Hussein judgment on deletions as limited to proceedings against individual electors.

items.title: Supreme Court wants cases of SIR excluded to be decided before next polls. A reality check from Assam
items.shows: It sets the Supreme Court's direction that exclusions be decided before the next polls against Assam's record. About 3 lakh voters were marked 'Doubtful' in a 1997 revision and 93,000 'D' voters remained before the 2026 Assembly election, with cases held up in Foreigners Tribunals and courts.

items.title: Citizen’s Handbook for Filing SIR Voter Deletion Appeals
items.authors: Sarfaraz Ahmed Khan, Tarique Quasimuddin, Darshana Mitra, Sabir Ahamed
items.shows: It is a step-by-step guide to appealing a deletion from West Bengal's roll before the 19 appellate tribunals set up after the Supreme Court's order, with sample appeals for nine common situations.

items.title: Is ECI Correct In Saying Supreme Court Upheld Its New Form 6 Declaration?
items.shows: It examines whether the May 2026 judgment actually considered the declaration the Commission later added to Form 6, as the Commission claimed.

items.title: Powers of the CEC | Day 1: SC seeks ECI’s response on plea
items.shows: It reports the hearing in which the Court issued notice to the Commission and all three Commissioners on petitions alleging the Chief Election Commissioner took decisions alone, and declined to suspend him in the interim. The Chief Justice said no modified Form 6 had been approved by the Court.

items.title: RTI Reveals: In SIR, Purging of ‘Ineligibles’ from the Voter Lists Might be a Bogey
items.shows: The author asked the Election Commission and the Home Ministry under the RTI Act on 10 August 2026 whether the Commission had referred electors it found not to be citizens to the competent authority under the Citizenship Act, as the Supreme Court ordered in May 2026 to be done within four weeks. The Commission replied after 50 days that it held none of the information. The Home Ministry transferred its application the same day to the Legislative Department, which sent it on to the Commission, and the Commission then passed the questions to the Home Ministry and to the Chief Electoral Officer of Bihar. No reply named the competent authority or gave a number of cases referred.

items.title: ‘Do not put words in our mouth’: Supreme Court says it never adjudicated new Form 6, will examine challenge on Oct 27
items.shows: It reports the bench clarifying that it neither approved nor disapproved the declaration added to Form 6, because it did not exist when the Bihar judgment was given. It sets out the Commission's 26 September claim, the rule-making route under Section 28 of the 1950 Act, and the listing of the challenge for 27 October.

items.title: In India, a Dark Shadow Falls on Its Vaunted Elections
items.shows: It is a lawyer's essay for an international readership on the protests in Delhi on 10 and 12 October 2026 and how the SIR reached them. It argues that the Supreme Court let the revision become a fact on the ground before ruling on it, then upheld it in 2026 and, in the author's view, freed the Commission from having to act proportionately, and that the Commission's independence was never secured in law. It cites the 90% of decided West Bengal appeals that restored the elector and the Indian Express investigation into the two Commissioners' objections.

items.title: SIR Enumeration Form may have violated electoral rules prescribing Form-4 for collecting voter details
items.shows: It sets the enumeration form used in the revision beside Rule 8 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, which prescribes Form 4 for collecting electors' details from households, and Rule 25, which says an intensively revised roll is prepared afresh. The form came pre-printed from the 2025 roll and asks for links to the 2002 roll, which Form 4 does not. Telangana's Chief Electoral Officer replied that Form 4 had not been used for a long time and that the format followed the Commission's decision.

items.title: Election Commission’s SIR Damage Control
items.shows: It goes through the measures the Commission announced from 26 September, among them the review of ECINET, the Form 6 declaration in the period outside the SIR, the cap on Form 7 applications of 9 October, and the Special Summary Revision with draft and final rolls in PDF for parties at no cost. It sets them beside the two Election Commissioners' objections and the Cabinet Secretariat's RTI reply, with comments from former Chief Election Commissioner O.P. Rawat, Maj Gen Anil Verma (Retd) of ADR and a co-founder of Voter Adhikar Manch.

items.title: Guidebook: SIR (Special Intensive Revision)
items.outlet: Part III Action Research & Resource Centre
items.shows: Part III Action Research & Resource Centre, a legal aid group with offices in New Delhi and Patna, wrote this guide for Delhi's electors and says it grew out of helping survivors of domestic violence apply in the revision. It covers who is eligible, the enumeration form on paper or online, finding a name in the draft roll and in Delhi's list of notices, Forms 6, 7 and 8, the documents to keep ready, hearings and the two appeals. It gives the 1950 helpline, the Commission's complaint routes and where to go for help without the internet. Its dates for Delhi are the ones the Commission set on 29 October, with claims and objections until 25 November, notices decided by 15 December and the final roll on 22 December. Its table of forms gives Form 7 for an elector whose own name was wrongly deleted. Form 7 is the form for objecting to a name on the roll, and the Commission's Manual on Electoral Rolls of 2023 says a person no longer on the roll applies again on Form 6. The guide is in English and Hindi.

items.title: EC says decisions were unanimous but leaves a big question unanswered
items.shows: The Indian Express reads the Election Commission's affidavit of 26 October 2026 in the Supreme Court against the 14 notes by Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi that its investigation reported. By the paper's account, the affidavit says the Commission's decisions on the revision were taken collectively and that a Commissioner's note is not itself a decision, accepts that steps taken by officers on the online Form 6 needed to be corrected, sets out a review of ECINet by a committee with experts from IIT Mumbai and IISc Bengaluru, and says 88 of the 97 Goa electors left off the final roll have since applied through Form 6. The paper says most of the notes were written after decisions had been taken, and that the affidavit does not say who approved the online change to Form 6 in July, does not mention Joshi's proposal of 29 May for such a committee, and does not say why an order redistributing work in July was issued without the Commission.

items.title: Form 6, voter roll deletions: What Election Commission told the Supreme Court
items.shows: The Indian Express explains what the Election Commission's affidavit of 26 October 2026 in the Supreme Court means for electors. It sets the affidavit's account of the online Form 6 beside the paper's report of 12 July that a declaration about the last intensive revision had been inserted within the form for every state, and beside the Commission's press note of 26 September. By the paper's account, the Commission decided on 21 October that the online application will be in two parts, so that a new elector can apply through Form 6 without the declaration, which remains a separate requirement where a revision is under way. It also sets out the West Bengal appeals, of which, by the Commission's data, 16.10 lakh were filed against orders of the judicial officers that put names back on the roll, and the affidavit's account of how the Commission takes decisions.

items.title: ECI’s stand that additional declaration is not part of Form 6 comes days after SC said it will examine ‘new’ Form 6
items.shows: Krishnadas Rajagopal reads the Election Commission's affidavit, which says the additional declaration is not part of the statutory Form 6, against the Supreme Court's oral remark of 12 October that the new Form 6 was neither approved nor disapproved in the Bihar judgment and that the Court would examine it. He sets out the petitioners' argument that electors deleted in the revision are made to apply again as fresh voters through Form 6, and the Commission's reply that the declaration let electors give their details in a single document.

items.title: ECI affidavit to Court has unresolved questions, unbroken silences
items.shows: The Indian Express's editorial calls the Commission's affidavit of 26 October 2026 underwhelming and says it raises more questions than it answers. By the paper's account the affidavit treats the 14 objections Election Commissioners Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu recorded in 10 months as part of the consultative process, while most of them were about orders already issued and decisions taken without the two being told. The editorial says the affidavit rolls back the changes made to Form 6 for first-time voters online and sets up a committee that includes experts to review whether ECINet complies with the law, without acknowledging the mistake or holding anyone accountable. It notes that 88 of the 97 Goa voters left off the final rolls have since applied through Form 6, and asks why the software blocked, in February, the registration officers' decisions to reverse the deletions. On West Bengal it says the affidavit names the office of the state's Chief Electoral Officer as the filer of appeals against orders restoring voters, and asks why the two Commissioners were kept in the dark when they asked about it earlier. It cites the paper's report that judges of the tribunals the Court appointed to decide SIR appeals in West Bengal say the Commission's requirement for Aadhaar authentication in its portal is in their way, and asks the Supreme Court to nudge the Commission towards a course correction that begins with fuller transparency.

items.title: Five Reasons Why the ECI’s Explanation for 16 Lakh Appeals Against Bengal Voters Falls Short
items.shows: Aparna Bhattacharya reads paragraph 63 of the Commission's counter-affidavit of 26 October 2026, which says that officers of the office of West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer filed the appeals against 16.10 lakh voters cleared by judicial officers, in their capacity as authorities under the Representation of the People Act. She sets out five problems with that account. The appellate tribunals were created by the Supreme Court and do not exist under the Act, and the orders of 1 April and 6 April 2026 that the affidavit quotes name no officer. The affidavit lists the CEO, DEOs, EROs and AEROs as the authorities for the rolls and does not say that any of them filed the appeals. Appeal records collected by the Civic Research Group and analysed by The Wire show more than 12 lakh of the appeals in one batch lodged on 5 April, a day before the order of 6 April. The affidavit describes these voters as already on the rolls with orders in their favour and gives no ground for challenging them. The piece reports that hearing notices of one tribunal in Murshidabad record the appeal as filed by the Additional CEO, and quotes Prasenjit Bose, who chairs the West Bengal Congress SIR committee, calling the appeals prima facie unauthorised and illegal and asking for a judicial probe.

items.title: Six Ways EC Affidavit Ends Up Reinforcing Doubts About SIR Irregularities and Commission's Functioning
items.shows: Sravasti Dasgupta reads the Commission's affidavit of 26 October 2026 against The Indian Express's reports that Election Commissioners Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu objected 14 times in ten months, and finds that it denies none of those findings. By her account the affidavit says the Commission neither released nor authorised the release of any internal note, and that all three orders for the SIR were reached unanimously. It denies that Form 6 was amended while accepting that the declaration was entered into the online page of the form, and it now calls the declaration a separate and independent document, where a press note of the month before had said the declaration attached to Form 6 was upheld by the Supreme Court. She writes that on Goa it says 88 of the 97 voters have applied again through Form 6 and does not explain why registration officers could not restore them, and that on West Bengal it says the appeals were not brought to the Commission. It announces a committee with experts from IIT Mumbai and IISc Bengaluru to review new ECINet modules without mentioning that Joshi had proposed one, and it calls the allegations drawn from the two Commissioners' letters to the Cabinet Secretary about a work allocation order misconceived, saying the order was never implemented.

items.title: The SIR verdict, serious constitutional questions
items.shows: Bishwajit Bhattacharyya, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court and a former Additional Solicitor General of India, argues that the Court erred in its verdict of 27 May 2026 by allowing the Commission a limited inquiry into citizenship when it includes or deletes names. In his reading the words limited and strict sense carry no legal significance, and the holding that the Commission's power affects an individual's entitlement to be on the roll can only mean that it may disenfranchise an existing voter. He says the Commission's role in preparing the roll is ministerial, that the verdict named no document as proof of citizenship, and that a qualified voter can be disqualified only on the grounds in Article 326 and only after a hearing. He asks how a roll used in a concluded election can be altered on suspicion, urges the Court to lay down a yardstick for establishing citizenship, and reads three earlier judgments as making the right to vote a basic feature of the Constitution.

items.title: Deemed ineligible: On the Supreme Court and SIR
items.shows: The Hindu's editorial takes up Justice Joymalya Bagchi's question at the Delhi hearing of 28 October, whether an elector who was lax or did not respond to the enumeration form should lose the vote for ever, and calls the shift of the burden of enrolment from the state to the elector the central design flaw of the SIR. It gives the share of names left off the draft as shifted or absent as 55% in Bihar and 72% in the third phase, and says Karnataka's final roll is 64.5 lakh short of the projected adult population after about 84 lakh were marked shifted or absent and a net 8.2 lakh were added during claims. It recalls that in the 2002 to 2003 revision enumerators enrolled shifted voters at their new homes. It says no statute or rule allows a voter's eligibility to be judged by family size or the age gap with a parent, and asks the Court to go beyond extended deadlines, to put back electors wrongly left off the draft and to settle the questions over the Commission's conduct and the appointment of its members.

items.title: Election Commission’s appeals against 16.10 lakh cleared voters raise legal questions
items.shows: The Hindu asks whether the officials who filed 16,10,311 appeals against West Bengal electors cleared by judicial officers had the power to do so. The Representation of the People Act names the Chief Electoral Officer, District Election Officers and registration officers as the authorities for the roll. The Commission's affidavit of 26 October calls the appellants officers of the Chief Electoral Officer's office and says a letter of 22 October from that office claimed the authority as officers under the Act and under the Supreme Court's orders, without saying the appeals were filed by those named authorities. It gives Prasenjit Bose's argument that no one can have authority under the Act before tribunals the Act does not mention, which were set up on the Supreme Court's direction in 2026, and the Congress memorandum of 29 October to the Chief Electoral Officer asking for the appeals to be cancelled and for an IT audit of when and how they were filed. It sets out the numbers. Of about 60 lakh doubtful cases, judicial officers cleared 32,77,360 and rejected 27.23 lakh, 22 lakh of those rejected appealed, and with the Commission's appeals more than 38 lakh cases were pending.

items.title: Epic failures: on electoral roll, welfare
items.shows: The Hindu's editorial takes up the statement of Rajiv Ranjan Singh, the Union Minister of Panchayati Raj, that voter identity cards with biometric authentication will replace Aadhaar in identifying beneficiaries and making payments under his Ministry's schemes, and says it runs contrary to existing laws and regulations. It recalls the Supreme Court's judgment of 27 May on the Bihar SIR, which allowed the Commission only a limited enquiry into citizenship whose consequences are confined to the roll and the vote, and which called the EPIC a derivative document issued on the basis of inclusion in the roll. It also recalls the Court's observations on petitions against West Bengal's orders removing people deleted from the roll from the Public Distribution System and the Annapurna Yojana. It says 93% of the appeals heard in West Bengal for reinstatement had ended with names restored by September 2026, and that the Court has yet to decide whether the Commission's method of logical discrepancies is lawful. It argues that the BJP-led coalition sees the smaller rolls as a way to limit welfare, and asks the Court to decide the petitions against the SIR and to say again that its rolls cannot be used to curtail welfare.

items.title: ECI and its black box: How the election body denies the right to know
items.shows: Venkatesh Nayak, director of the Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative, writes that he asked the Commission under the RTI Act in May 2026 for the reports of the Chief Electoral Rolls Observers it sent to 12 states and union territories in the second phase of the SIR, West Bengal among them. He says the Commission refused, citing a decision of the Central Information Commission of 2010. He says it refused his earlier request for the reports of its Expenditure Observers from the 2024 Lok Sabha election on the same ground and sent him its internal circulars of 2016 and 2022, which list observers' reports among the information to be refused under the Act. He argues that most exemptions in the Act carry a test of harm, that the 2010 decision accepted the Commission's claims of a fiduciary relationship with its observers and of danger to them without question and made no mention of S P Gupta v. President of India (1981), and that information commissioners since have not weighed the public interest as the Act requires. He opens with the claim of the former Special Roll Observer for West Bengal that the observer had no prior knowledge of the Chief Electoral Officer's appeals against electors the judicial officers had cleared, and with the Commission's statement to the Court that it had only a communication after the appeals were filed.

items.title: ECI’s belated U-turn doesn’t undo the injustice of mass exclusions
items.authors: Anjali Bhardwaj, Amrita Johri, Yogendra Yadav
items.shows: Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri, RTI activists with the Satark Nagrik Sangathan and the NCPRI who are petitioners on the Delhi SIR in the Supreme Court, and Yogendra Yadav of Swaraj India and the Bharat Jodo Abhiyan, read the Commission's letter of 6 November to the Chief Electoral Officers of Delhi, Maharashtra, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Jharkhand, Telangana and Nagaland. By their account it waives the deadline for enumeration forms in those seven states and lets an elector who has moved come back to the roll on the enumeration form with a new address in place of Form 6. It lets a homeless elector be added on a field check by the booth level officer. It invokes Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, under which a registration officer can correct a name left out by inadvertence or error, and it gives a restored elector the old EPIC number. They give 4.52 crore names left off the draft in the seven states and 13.3 crore across India. They tie the letter to the Supreme Court's hearing of 28 October, when the bench called the use of Form 6 for such electors an error and a structural incongruity, and they set it beside the Commission's clarification of 3 November that a Form 6 filed by such an elector would not be treated as a false declaration. They ask why the same relief is not open in Bengaluru or in states such as Bihar and West Bengal where the revision is over, and whether electors who have already filed Form 6 will get their old numbers back. They argue that the revision still places on the elector the burden of being on the roll and that it should be withdrawn.

items.title: Explainer: Can the SIR Be Rectified?
items.shows: Rangarajan R., a former IAS officer, sets out the Supreme Court's judgment of May 2026 upholding the revision in Bihar and asks whether the revision can be put right. In his summary the court held that the Commission may revise the roll for many or all constituencies of a state under section 21(3) of the Representation of the People Act read with Article 324, that the measures are proportionate and keep the safeguards of notice and hearing, and that the Commission may make a limited enquiry into citizenship for the purpose of the roll, with any deletion on grounds of citizenship referred to the competent authority under the Citizenship Act, 1955. He sets the revision beside the Commission's guidelines of May 2002 for the last intensive revision, under which supervisors were to check at least 25% of the households at random, electors who had moved were enrolled at their new address in the same exercise, and claims and objections filed in bulk were to be rejected summarily. In the present revision, he writes, the notification issued before Bihar's revision asks supervisors for 10% random verification, an elector marked shifted has to apply on Form 8 at the new address or afresh on Form 6, and the Commission capped the objection forms one person may file at 10 only on 9 October 2026. He writes that 71% of those deleted across the three phases fall under the Absent, Shifted or Others category and that many of them could be eligible to enrol again once the revision is complete, and that software flags of logical discrepancies, among them spelling differences, more than six voters linked to one ancestor and gaps of age between parent and child outside 15 to 45 years, led to the arbitrary exclusion of lakhs of eligible voters. For West Bengal he writes that more than 22 lakh appeals for inclusion had been filed and around 1.2 lakh decided by October 2026, and that of 83,000 decided by August the tribunals allowed around 75,000. He proposes a detailed audit of the final rolls, the use of the special summary revision ordered in 14 states and three union territories to enrol again those wrongly left out, and house-to-house enumeration as a requirement wherever a revision is under way, with the rolls finalised only after all claims and objections are decided.

items.title: A chance to undo SIR’s wrongs
items.shows: Deccan Herald's editorial says the special summary revision in the states where the intensive revision has ended is an opportunity to repair the damage it says the intensive revision did. It gives Karnataka's electorate as falling from 5.54 crore to 4.55 crore after the intensive revision, more than 99 lakh fewer names, with the final roll of the summary revision due on 20 January 2027. It says the Commission has clarified that voters need not establish a link with the rolls of 2002, and reads that as an admission that the intensive revision imposed unreasonable burdens on voters. It says the remedy comes too late for voters in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Bihar, where the revision was held close to the elections, and that in West Bengal nearly 21 lakh appeals against deletions remain pending months after polling. It asks Karnataka's parties to use their booth level agents to see that every eligible voter is restored to the rolls, and says the Congress did not sustain its campaign. It notes the Karnataka High Court's stay of the investigations in the FIRs against BJP booth level agents accused of filing Form 7 objections in bulk, says the court's view that the registration officer must first complete the statutory process may be legally defensible, and sets beside it the Commission's acknowledgement of more than 91,000 Form 7 applications, many in bulk, and its position that no voter has been deleted on them. It asks that the Commission's new safeguards, among them scrutiny of bulk objections, hearings and reasoned orders before any deletion, be enforced in the summary revision.

items.title: Watch: Bihar SIR: The mystery behind 7 lakh more women elector deletions | Data Point
items.shows: The Hindu's data team sets the gender gap among the names left off Bihar's draft against census migration records and the ages of those left off.

items.title: विशेष गहन पुनरीक्षण: वोटर लिस्ट की सफ़ाई के वादे पर वोट देने के मूल अधिकार की कब्र खोदने का इंतज़ाम
items.shows: It is a Hindi video version of the Collective's Electoral Roll Project findings. Uploaded 5 March 2026, Pacific time (6 March IST).

items.title: Inside The Election Commission: Investigation Finds ECs Split On Key Issues | Indian Express Special
items.shows: It is the paper's video account of its investigation into the Election Commission. Two Election Commissioners objected on file at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions they said were taken without their knowledge, on deletions, additions, appeals and access to ERONET and ECINET. It also covers the questions added to Form 6, the 97 Goa electors officials could not restore, and the 16 lakh appeals the Commission told the Supreme Court were filed in West Bengal against restored voters.

items.title: Two ECs dissent, questions on legality of SIR process: Constitutional, legal issues & nuances
items.shows: Shekhar Gupta goes through the Indian Express report of the two Election Commissioners' 14 objections, what it shows and what it does not, and the constitutional and legal questions it raises.

items.title: Election Commission Investigation: Ritika Chopra Answers All Your Questions On ECI Investigation
items.shows: The editor who led the paper's investigation into the two Commissioners' objections answers readers' questions on how the software-made 'logical discrepancy' category works, why objections on file by two of three members matter under the law, and what the Commission's reply did and did not deny.

items.title: SIR: 8 Questions, 8 Clear Answers | Election Facts | BJP
items.shows: It is the BJP's own account of the SIR, answering eight questions on topics the party lists as the 13 crore names, Form 6, ECINET, young voters, the role of the Election Commissioners, 'vote chori' and AI. Its description cites the Commission's published material as saying the SIR is meant to include eligible voters and drop ineligible entries, with claims, objections and appeals, and gives Bihar's final roll as about 7.42 crore.

items.title: “13 Crore Voters Deleted?”| The Real SIR Numbers Explained | #SIR | #BJP
items.shows: It is a BJP short on the 13 crore names left off the drafts. Its description splits them, citing the Commission's figures, into absent, shifted or other (9.5 crore, 71%), dead (2.7 crore, 20%) and duplicate (1 crore, 7.6%), argues that, given that split, the 13 crore cannot all be read as eligible voters deleted, and points to the Commission's drive to enrol eligible voters who were left out.

items.title: More SIR Deletions, Bigger BJP Swing? Prannoy Roy DeKodes the Data | DeKoder
items.shows: Prannoy Roy sets the names West Bengal left off or deleted beside the 2026 swing against the TMC and argues that they enlarged it. The episode shows no allowance for other differences between seats, and the other analyses of the same question listed here reach different answers.

items.title: Gyanesh Kumar Row: How did the ECI delete 13 crore voters during the SIR | Insight India
items.shows: It is a conversation with The Hindu's Srinivasan Ramani on how more than 13 crore names came off draft rolls in 30 states and UTs, what the data says about who was left off, and the questions about the exercise's legality.

items.title: Focus on inclusion made Kerala SIR credible | Onmanorama Explains
items.shows: It walks through Kerala's figures. The final roll is 8,97,211 below the 2024 roll (3.24 per cent), more than 98 per cent of the 36.89 lakh unmapped or discrepant electors were kept after hearings, and 92.7 per cent of 14.57 lakh Form 6 applications were accepted. Booth-level officers told the channel they were asked to include as many voters as possible.

items.title: Dhruv Rathee Interviews Former Chief Election Commissioner | Dr. S.Y. Quraishi
items.shows: A conversation in Hindi with S.Y. Quraishi, Chief Election Commissioner from 2010 to 2012. He says that after the revision of 2002 and 2003 the rolls were kept up to date by summary revision, with a booth level officer visiting each home and citizenship taken on the elector's own declaration in Form 6. He says almost every decision under the present Chief Election Commissioner is his alone, though the law asks for unanimity as far as possible and a majority otherwise. He argues that Form 6 cannot lawfully be used to bring back electors deleted in the revision, because it carries a declaration that the applicant has never been enrolled, and proposes a separate form approved by the Law Ministry. He also says the West Bengal election should be held again because it was held on a roll he regards as unlawful. He criticises the Supreme Court for letting that election go ahead and for sending judicial officers to do the Commission's work.

items.title: SIR in West Bengal: How Were 90 Lakh Voter Names Deleted? | Prasenjit Bose Explains
items.shows: Frontline's Suhrid Sankar Chattopadhyay talks with Prasenjit Bose, who chairs the SIR panel of the West Bengal Pradesh Congress Committee and moved the Supreme Court after the state's Assembly election. Bose argues that Muslim electors were deleted out of proportion to their share and that the BJP would not have won its majority without the deletions. Citing figures he says the Commission gave in reply to his petition, he puts the Form 6 applications in the state at about 34 lakh, of which about 20 per cent, some 7 lakh, were accepted and about 20 lakh were still pending in August. Against that he puts about 6.3 lakh Form 7 applications, of which about 90 per cent, some 5.7 lakh, led to deletions. He says the tribunals hold about 38 lakh cases, about 22 lakh of them appeals by electors deleted after adjudication and about 16 lakh appeals against electors whom judicial officers found eligible, and that 93 per cent of the about 1.26 lakh cases decided so far went in favour of inclusion. He asks that the 22 lakh be restored before their cases are heard, so that they can vote in the coming municipal elections, that the 16 lakh appeals be cancelled, and that electors with appeals pending be allowed to apply through Form 6 as deleted electors in other states can. He says faults in the ECINET and ERONET portals are slowing the tribunals, and calls for a judicial inquiry and a forensic audit of both portals in every state where the revision has been held.

items.title: Prashant Bhushan on SIR, Youth Protests and Opposition Politics
items.shows: It is Amit Baruah's SpeakEasy conversation with the senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, recorded before the INDIA bloc rally of 1 November. Bhushan argues that electors who moved house were made to return through Form 6, which he says asks the applicant to declare that they have never voted before, when Form 8 for shifted electors would have kept their EPIC number. He says he would not sign such a declaration even with an assurance that no one would be prosecuted for it. He proposes that a revision be done through ward and gram sabhas at each booth, with the old roll read aloud and the meeting filmed, and says this was once done in several areas of Rajasthan. He says he suspects that the method for flagging logical discrepancies was designed to single out Muslim electors, and gives as his reason that two thirds of those flagged in West Bengal were Muslim in a state where Muslims are 27 per cent of the population. He criticises the Commission's affidavit on how the decision to hold the revision across the country was taken, and cites an RTI reply to Anjali Bhardwaj that he says shows no record of such a decision. He calls for the revision to be scrapped, the rolls from before it to be restored and the elections held on its rolls to be scrapped too, which he says he does not expect to happen. The second half of the conversation is about the youth protests, the opposition parties and the place of money in elections.

items.title: Inside Telangana’s SIR: Lakhs deleted, millions served notices
items.shows: It is a documentary report by Frontline on the revision in Telangana, reported and scripted by Ayesha Minhaz. It says the state had about 3.38 crore electors when the revision began on 15 June and 2.65 crore on the draft roll of 17 August, and that nearly 73 lakh names were left off the draft as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate. It says nearly 93 lakh electors on the draft, about 35 per cent of it, received notices over logical discrepancies or because they could not be mapped to the 2002 roll, for reasons that included a small spelling mismatch, an age gap between a parent and a child judged too small, and several children mapped to the same parent. In Hyderabad's constituencies the report says many booth level officers rarely visited homes. It meets electors who say they handed in their enumeration forms and were still listed as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate, electors marked permanently shifted who still live at the address on the roll, and electors marked dead without a visit. It describes Form 6 with a declaration linking the elector to the 2002 roll as the way back, Form 6 applications rejected without reasons, and the bulk Form 7 applications in at least four Hyderabad constituencies, and it says the Chief Electoral Officer has yet to disclose more than 70 per cent of the Form 7 applications filed in the state.
